utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-A, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Brahimaj, I am to ask you whether you can hear me and whether you can follow the proceedings through the translation. Are you hearing me?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT BRAHIMAJ
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And we will now have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Peter Kremer appearing on behalf of the Prosecution. I'm assisted this morning by Ms. Martin Salgado and Mr. Marwan Dalal, and to my left our case manager Colin Nawrot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kremer. And for Mr. Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. My name is Ben Emmerson, and I appear together with Mr. Rodney Dixon for Mr. Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Gregor Guy-Smith, I appear with Ms. Colleen Rohan and Mr. Chad Mair on behalf of Idriz Balaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And thanks for the correction in the translation, Balaj. I think I have it now. Now, Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. My name is Richard Harvey. I appear together with Mr. Paul Troop, Ms. Antoniette Trapani, and Ms. Rudina Jasini on behalf of Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. This is the appeals hearing in the case of the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj, and Lahi Brahimaj. I will briefly summarise the appeals and the manner in which we will proceed. Both Mr. Brahimaj and the Prosecution have appealed the trial judgement rendered on the 3rd of April, 2008, by Trial Chamber I composed of Judge Alphonse Orie presiding and Judges Frank Hoepfel and Ole Bjorn Stole. The Trial Chamber found the evidence before it insufficient to establish the existence of a joint criminal enterprise in which the three accused participated. It acquitted all three accused of Counts 6, 14, 20, 22, 30, 36, and 37 of the indictment. It further acquitted Mr. Haradinaj and Mr. Balaj of Counts 28 and 32 and held that Mr. Brahimaj would not be held responsible under Counts 28 and 32 of the indictment as a participant in a joint criminal enterprise. The Chamber acquitted Mr. Haradinaj and Mr. Balaj of all alternative charges in the indictment. It found Mr. Brahimaj guilty of torture as a violation of the laws or customs of war charged in Count 28 of the indictment and torture and cruel treatment as violations of the laws or customs of war as charged in Count 32 of the indictment. The Chamber found Mr. Brahimaj not guilty under all other counts in the indictment and sentenced Mr. Brahimaj to a single sentence of six years' of imprisonment. Let me start by recounting Mr. Brahimaj's appeal. Mr. Brahimaj requests the Trial Chamber to reverse his convictions in relation to the torture and cruel treatment of Witnesses 3 and 6 under Counts 28 and 32 of the indictment. Further, or in the alternative, Mr. Brahimaj seeks the reduction of his sentence and he sets fourth 19 grounds of appeal. First ground, he argues that in finding that he personally participated in the cruel treatment and torture of Witness 6, the Chamber committed errors of fact and law by failing to take into account or failing to give proper reasons for rejecting fundamental issues relating to Witness's 6's credibility. In his second ground, he contends that the Trial Chamber erred in law and fact in concluding that Witness 6 was tortured in order to punish him for his perceived collaboration with Serbs and to discriminate against him on political grounds. In his third and fourth grounds of appeal, he alleges that in finding him guilty of torture and cruel treatment in relation to Witness 3, the Chamber failed to properly apply the standards of proof beyond a reasonable doubt and in dubio pro reo and failed to sufficiently address conflicts between the evidence of Witnesses 3 and 6. In his fifth ground of appeal, Mr. Brahimaj contends that the Trial Chamber committed errors of fact and law by failing to properly assess the reliability and credibility of Witness 3. In his sixth ground of appeal, Mr. Brahimaj asserts that the Chamber committed errors of law and fact when assessing the testimony of Witness 3 in relation to his return to Jablanica. In his seventh and eighth ground of appeal, he avers that in finding that he was responsible for the cruel treatment and torture of Witness 3 under Count 32 of the indictment, the Chamber failed to clearly specify whether or not it intended to convict him of the first alleged beating of Witness 3; and if so, it failed to give reasons for its conclusions and committed errors of fact. In his ninth ground of appeal, he argues that the Chamber erred in law and fact in concluding that the reason for Witness 3's mistreatment was to punish him for withholding a weapon and for his perceived ties to Serbs. Further, or in the alternative, Mr. Brahimaj contends that the Prosecution has failed to prove one or more of the material elements of the charge of torture. In grounds 10 through 19, Mr. Brahimaj challenges his sentence of six years of imprisonment, submitting that the Chamber made numerous errors of law and fact in determining this to be an appropriate sentence. Specifically, he asserts that the Chamber erred in, one, finding that his previously held positions of authority amounted to an aggravating factor; two, finding that his position as a member of the KLA General Staff was a high-ranking position in the KLA and an aggravating factor; three, finding that his previous appointment as deputy commander of the Dukagjin zone amounted to a high-ranking position within the KLA and was thus an aggravating factor; four, finding that his presence had to have an encouraging effect on the soldiers to commit crimes; five, finding that he committed crimes in the presence of lower-ranking soldiers; six, finding the special vulnerability of Witnesses 3 and 6 to be an aggravating factor; finding that Witness 6 was still suffering from physical trauma, constituting an aggravating factor; eight, finding that Witness 3 was still suffering physical and mental trauma; nine, finding that upon learning of the death of Skender Kuci, Witness 6 became more fearful for his life, constituting an aggravating factor; and ten, failing to correctly exercise its discretion in imposing a sentence that was manifestly excessive under the circumstances. In its response, the Prosecution argues that Mr. Brahimaj's appeal should be dismissed in its entirety. I turn now to the Prosecution's appeal. The Prosecution requests the Appeals Chamber to reverse the Trial Chamber's decisions to acquit Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj, Lahi Brahimaj of criminal responsibility based on joint criminal enterprise liability for crimes committed at the KLA headquarters and the prison in Jablanica under Counts 24, 26, 28, 30, 32, and 34 of the indictment, as well as of individual criminal responsibility under Counts 24 and 34 of the indictment, and to reverse the Trial Chamber's decision to acquit Lahi Brahimaj of individual criminal responsibility under Count 26 of the indictment. It requests the Appeals Chamber to remit these matters to a Trial Chamber for a re-trial on these counts. It also asks the Trial Chamber -- it also requests the Appeals Chamber to reverse the acquittal of Idriz Balaj for murder and enter a conviction against him under Count 14 of the indictment for murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war under Article 3 of the Statute, for having aided and abetted the murders of sister S, the mother of Witness 4, and sister M, and to sentence Idriz Balaj accordingly. Furthermore, the Prosecution requests the Trial Chamber to reverse Idriz Balaj's acquittal and convict him under Counts 36 and 37 of the indictment for the rape, torture, and cruel treatment of Witness 61, as well as the cruel treatment of Witness 1, as violations of the laws or customs of war under Article 3 of the Statute and to sentence him accordingly. It sets out three grounds of appeal. In its first ground it argues that the Trial Chamber erred in law by denying the Prosecution its right to a fair trial under Article 20(1) of the Statute, when the Trial Chamber failed to grant it additional time to exhaust all reasonable steps to secure the testimony of two crucial witnesses and ordered the Prosecution's case closed before such reasonable steps could be taken. In its second ground of appeal, the Prosecution asserts that in acquitting Idriz Balaj of aiding and abetting the commission of the murders of sister S, the mother of Witness 4, and sister M under Count 14 the Chamber erred in law or in fact when it held that the mens rea and the actus reus of aiding and abetting were not satisfied. In its third ground, the Prosecution contends that the Trial Chamber erred in fact and law in finding that Idriz Balaj was not responsible for the rape, torture, and cruel treatment of Witness 61 and the cruel treatment of Witness 1. In their responses, Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj, and Lahi Brahimaj submit that the appeal against the Trial Chamber's verdict of acquittal in their respective cases should be dismissed and the judgement of the Trial Chamber affirmed. The parties of course may argue the grounds of appeal in the order they consider most suitable for their presentation. But I urge them not to simply repeat verbatim or summarise extensively what is already set out in the briefs, as the Court is aware of the contents of the briefs and has studied them. The hearing will proceed according to the Scheduling Order issued on the 25th of August, 2009. The Prosecution presents its submissions this morning for one hour and 20 minutes, and then we have a 30-minute pause. Counsel for Haradinaj will have 55 minutes to respond. Counsel for Mr. Balaj, 55 minutes. Then there will be a one-hour pause, and subsequently counsel for Mr. Brahimaj will have 55 minutes to respond. And the Prosecution will then have 30 minutes to present its replies. After a 15-minute pause, counsel for Mr. Brahimaj will present his submissions for one hour and a 20 minutes, followed by a 30-minute pause. The Prosecution will then present its response for 55 minutes. Afterwards, counsel for Mr. Brahimaj will have 30 minutes to reply, and then we'll have 15 minutes reserved for Mr. Brahimaj to present a personal statement, should he so desire. Let us now begin by hearing the Prosecution, Mr. Kremer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, I will present the Prosecution's submissions on ground one, and my colleague Ms. Martin Salgado will present our submissions on ground three and will be available for questions on ground two. Starting with ground one, the breach of the Prosecution's right to a fair trial under Article 20(1) of the Statute. The Trial Chamber's mandate under Article 20(1) of the Statute was to ensure that the trial was fair and expeditious. Article 20(1) also required that the proceedings were conducted with due regard for the protection of victims and witnesses. The Chamber had the discretion to apply the rules to ensure a fair trial. When confronted with evidence of massive witness intimidation in this case, the Trial Chamber could have shifted its priority from an expeditious trial to preserving a fair trial; it did not. It could have been more flexible in scheduling so justice could be done so the truth could be found; it did not. It could have abandoned its rigid course of applying the rules to compel attendance and considered alternative ways to receive the evidence of the intimidated witnesses; it did not. When the Trial Chamber closed the Prosecution case, faced with an extraordinary situation where two crucial witnesses had not testified because of intimidation, it was clearly in the interests of justice for the Trial Chamber to receive their evidence in written form under Rule 89(F). Their statements were highly credible, relevant, and probative. As to the use of the statements in the context of ensuring a fair trial to the Prosecution and to the Defence, the Trial Chamber could have used Rule 92 quater for guidance as to the conditions surrounding the receipt of this evidence. The Appeals Chamber in Tadic recognised that the Trial Chamber had an obligation to determine whether the Rules or the Statute could be used to relieve the situation when confronted with the complaining party bringing difficulties about witness attendance to the Trial Chamber's attention. I refer to appeal judgement paragraph 55. We say that this is consistent with the obligation of the Trial Chamber to use its powers to ensure a fair trial for both parties. The trial started on 5 March, 2007. The Prosecution case ended a mere six months later. Two months later, closing arguments were heard. The judgement was issued a little over two months after. The Trial Chamber achieved an expeditious trial. By then, witness intimidation had infected the trial and prevented receipt of the evidence of at least two crucial witnesses. The Trial Chamber was on notice of the witness intimidation and, we submit, had an obligation and the responsibility to attempt to relieve the situation. The Trial Chamber failed to take vigorous steps to ensure a fair trial in this case. As Mr. President has mentioned, our remedy requested on ground one is a re-trial limited to the JCE responsibility of the three respondents for the crimes at the site of the KLA headquarters and the prison at Jablanica and their individual responsibility under the counts mentioned in the notice of appeal. During the course of my submissions, I intend to refer to these counts as the Jablanica counts. These two witnesses had relevant and probative evidence to offer. Both were intimidated and refused to testify because of fear of the consequences of testifying. On June 5th, 2007, Shefqet Kabashi appeared and, after refusing protective measures, testified about his perception of witness protection measures in this case. He did not deny the contents of the statements he had given to the OTP investigators. He simply refused to testify as to his knowledge of the facts alleged in the indictment. I refer you to his testimony dated 5 June 2007, as quoted at paragraph 10 of our appeal brief: "I am disappointed, and not only disappointed, but certain things that should not happen and should not be done in modern world have happened. You, yourself, may not have come across such things, but there were persons who were asked questions as witnesses and whose names don't even appear on witness lists because they have been killed. I don't want protective measures because such measures do not exist in reality; they only exist within the bounds of this courtroom, not outside it." And that's at transcript 5439 to 5440, and that was said in open session. What Kabashi is clearly saying is that intimidation worked; the Trial Chamber's protective measures didn't. The same is true of the other witness. In a fax dated 3 July 2007, he described threats, which influenced him not to testify. The contents are quoted in paragraph 14 of our confidential appeal brief, and let me just remind you what he wrote, but to do that I should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you. Death threats directed to witnesses or against family members were common means used to intimidate witnesses not to testify that were reported to the Trial Chamber. In a recent judgement of this Chamber in Haraqija and Morina, the Chamber discussed the intimidation by Morina as -- of a protected witness, Witness 2, to prevent him from testifying in this case, the Haradinaj case. Protective measures did not protect Witness 2 from being contacted and intimidated to withdraw from testifying in the Haradinaj et al case. It was suggested to him that it would be wise - and I'm quoting here from paragraph 42 of the judgement: " ... since all of the witnesses had been killed." Witness 2 testified. This appeal is about the two crucial witnesses that did not testify, Shefqet Kabashi and the other witness. Their evidence was central to the Jablanica counts. Shefqet Kabashi was a former KLA member who had been stationed at Jablanica. He had recounted in his 24 October 2004 statement that Ramush Haradinaj visited the Jablanica KLA headquarters and prison regularly, accompanied by Idriz Balaj. He saw two Roma persons detained under suspicion of being Serb collaborators at the Jablanica prison and heard Lahi Brahimaj say that they should be "sent to Drenica," a known euphemism for execution. Lahi Brahimaj and Idriz Balaj and others beat detainees at the Jablanica prison, and he saw Lahi Brahimaj and Idriz Balaj beat prisoners at the Jablanica prison and stated that Idriz Balaj was particularly cruel and notorious. If we could just return for a moment to private session and that will be our last journey there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Kremer, I have two questions for you. At what point do you believe the Trial Chamber would have the right to end its attempts to secure testimony from these two recalcitrant witnesses? And secondly: Could you explain why and how you believe the Trial Chamber on the remand could obtain the testimony of these two witnesses should we remand the case to them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: In answer to the first question as to when it would be right for the Trial Chamber to end its attempts to secure the testimony of the witnesses, it depends on all of the circumstances. In this particular case, Shefqet Kabashi was still in a dialogue with the

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: logical conclusion. That never happened because the Trial Chamber refused to permit it. Whether at the end of the day his testimony could have been compelled, we don't know at present. But those were steps, the compulsion of testimony, contempt, and having people testify after they were brought here, after having been arrested for contempt, had been successful. Whether it would have been successful in his case is an open question. So in our brief we submit that the Trial Chamber could have taken through a small delay, or a month or two delay, steps to at least see through to its logical conclusion the attention of the testimony of these witnesses. With respect to the other witness, we concede that we did not do -- excuse me, take all of the same steps with respect to him that we had been able to take with Mr. Kabashi. Our position quite clearly in the brief is that by the end of the day, at the end of the trial, the Trial Chamber was so hostile towards the Prosecution attempts to have the witness -- the testimony of these witnesses heard because it was intent on finishing the trial, that it would have been futile to make any further applications and no further applications were made. That is what we say to when. When should a Trial Chamber make these decisions to give up? It depends on the information it has and what is reasonable under the circumstances. If it had done so, if it had said: It is a waste of time to hear these witnesses, our position is that it then should have considered in light of the very extraordinary circumstances of this case where witness intimidation had infected the trial from its beginning and even before, that it should have seriously considered receiving their evidence - that is, the written statements that they had provided to OTP investigators - under 89(F) and provided the appropriate cautions to its application of that evidence when applying it in its final determination. That never happened. That consideration was never taken, and our position is that when you have a serious situation of witness intimidation where a case cannot be presented, the obligation rests with the Trial Chamber and it's put squarely on the Trial Chamber under Article 20(1) to address the problem. It was a challenge that was clearly before the Trial Chamber and a challenge it was not up to and, as a result, the Prosecution case was never complete. The evidence of these crucial witnesses was never heard and acquittals resulted. In terms of the second question, how can we be certain whether these witnesses will testify, I can say that we have made informal inquiries -- or formal inquiries of the two countries where these witnesses are resident. I have had no formal responses. I have had an informal response by one of the countries advising that the witness is still resident there and is still living in the community. So he is available to be spoken to, but we have not spoken to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kremer, you claim that the Trial Chamber refused to sit after 7.00 p.m. in the evening and the days after that. Do you happen to know what was the reason for the Trial Chamber's decision to do that so as to deny your right for a fair trial? My second question is that so far as I know that you have plenty opportunity to raise this issue or even could file an interlocutory appeal against the decision made by the Trial Chamber in this aspect, but you didn't do so. As you know, a party cannot remain silent on the matters at trial only to return on the appeal to ask for a trial de novo. So I would like to -- I would like you to answer those two questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I will. I agree that a trial -- or a party should not and the jurisprudence is clear on that, an appeal will not be successful if the party has, as it were, sat in the bushes and waited until an appeal to raise an issue. Our position is that this is not what we are doing. There was an opportunity -- a second opportunity, as the facts show, to have the other witness brought before the Court and that took place on the 26th of November, 2007, where the witness, instead of being brought before the Court in the country where he lives, was hospitalised and was unclear as to how long that hospitalisation could take. The Chamber did not deal with that fact until -- in a way other than to say the Prosecution case is closed, you've had your opportunity. In terms of the 7.00 problem, there were no reasons given as to why the court could not sit after 7.00. It simply said it could not sit. The Prosecution said: Why don't we try to sit on Friday? That was not possible either. What we say and what will I -- what I will say during the course of my submission, it was the rigidity of the Trial Chamber in its approach to all matters of scheduling and of application of the procedures that was part of the cause. It was the rush to finish the case to create -- to have an expeditious trial, and it lost sight of its primary obligation: To provide the parties with a fair trial, particularly the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kremer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Pocar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: If I could just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I think we may need a redaction at line 14-15, I mentioned where Mr. Kabashi was living through the discussion of where his lawyer was, and perhaps that could be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Pocar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Kremer, you mentioned -- made a reference to Article 20(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal if I am correct, and is that your position that the Chamber respected its obligation to ensure that the trial is expeditious but did not respect the obligation to ensure that the trial is fair? But Article 20(1) continues saying that: "The Chamber should ensure that proceedings are conducted in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence ..." Now, is that also your position, that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence were violated? And what is your comment on this same provision when it says that: "The Trial Chamber shall ensure ..." all this "with full respect for the rights of the accused and due regard for the protection of victims and witnesses." Do you allow for the Chamber having considered that the protection of witnesses would, in this particular case, lead not to insist on getting the witnesses' testimony? Which is your position on this? Since you mentioned this provision, I wanted to have a full comment on the provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: We do agree that the article provides for both a fair and an expeditious trial, and our position is that this trial was expeditious and not fair. In terms of the proceedings to be conducted in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, we say that the procedures of the Rules were followed. Not all of them were followed. We would say that section 89(F) was not considered as an alternative under the circumstances of witness intimidation as a vehicle for having this evidence received. And what happened was that the trial was abruptly stopped on the 26th of November -- in fact, it was foreseen on the 20th of November when the Trial Chamber said that the Prosecution case is over but for the extraordinary circumstance of this other witness testifying by way of videolink. So that -- if you look at the procedures that were followed, yes, they were followed. In fact, our position is that they were too rigidly followed, that the Trial Chamber in light of the growing evidence of witness intimidation still looked at the Rules that it had grown accustom to in terms of ensuring witness attendance. It started with voluntary attendances, subpoenas, forced attendances. Some witnesses were arrested based on contempt citations and they came forward and testified. There was videolinks. A lot of different methods were used to try and get these witnesses to testify, but our position is, very simply, that when witness intimidation invades a trial, the Trial Chamber has an obligation to do more. Because from the very instance that witness intimidation becomes apparent, a fair trial is at risk. And you can't assess whether the trial will be fair until the trial is over. In this particular case at the end of the day, much evidence was received but important evidence was not. Critical evidence by the Trial Chamber's own admission, crucial evidence as to the Jablanica counts, and in the end the accused were acquitted, not because the Rules weren't followed, not because the Trial Chamber didn't apply protective measures, but because the protective measures, the Rules themselves, were inadequate to ensure that the evidence was received. And the one rule that could have ensured at least the evidence to be considered, 89(F), with some cautions to ensure that the Defence received a fair trial under the circumstances, was never considered and never put --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- a specific application for the accepting of the evidence under 89(F).

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: There was no application made by the Prosecution under 89(F). And our position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you saying that the Chamber should have a proprio motu?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes, at some point under Article 20(1), and I'll refer to the jurisprudence in a minute, the problem passed to the Chamber. This wasn't a Prosecution problem. It was a Prosecution problem from the point of view that our witnesses were being intimidated, but the Chamber has the powers to solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say that the case is as much the Chamber's case as it is the parties' case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: The Chamber in the end is there to ensure that the trial was fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, this evidence I understand from you, was central to the Prosecution's case. Had it been received under 89(F), there wouldn't have been any cross-examination. Am I correct then?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In those circumstances, what weight would the Chamber have been able to attach to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: It depends on the amount of corroboration that existed in respect of those cases, the individual counts and generally the joint criminal enterprise evidence. And depending on the nature and the quality of the corroboration, the Trial Chamber could have applied or given it much weight. And that was an assessment it never undertook --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you will be pointing us, I take it, to the evidence that would -- that you say corroborates the evidence of -- the statements of these two witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I -- it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't want to take you off your course if you are going to come to it, but it would seem to me to be an important part of your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I can say in summary, if one looks at the statements that were provided, and particularly the paragraphs that deal with the Jablanica prison camp, and compare it to the judgement and the evidence of the witnesses that testified, there is sufficient corroboration that their statements could have been given significant weight. That is our position. It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Is it your argument, Mr. Kremer, that admission of the evidence you're talking about, written evidence, under 89(F) would have really produced a different result in trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Absolutely. It would have produced a different result in trial. There was two witnesses, a KLA insider and a detainee, to testify about the participation and involvement of all three accused, both in beatings and in other activity, to show that Mr. Haradinaj was in charge of the Dukagjin zone, to show that Mr. Haradinaj was present when beatings were taken, that Mr. Balaj was beating prisoners in the detention centre. This is about a JCE II case and defining who the -- who had control of the prison and who ran it and who was inside it participating in the criminal activity. And that additional evidence, we say, would have been sufficient to cause the Trial Chamber to seriously look at finding joint criminal enterprise, common purpose, and making the other findings that it did not make and should have made. And secondly, there is sufficient evidence that is corroborated as to individual responsibility in respect of specific beatings. I agree, that with some of the counts they would only apply to the JCE crime because there are positive findings already that the KLA members at the prison were committing crimes against detainees, but there is additional evidence provided by both these witnesses as to crimes committed by the three respondents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Vaz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. I would first like to ask you, Mr. Kremer, whether you would be so kind as to point to the references in the paragraphs, tell us which paragraphs you're referring to in your submissions. This would be very helpful in our research. Secondly, I have a question. Earlier on you said that the Prosecutor was able to identify the whereabouts of one or even two witnesses, but that with regard to the latter the place of residence -- yes, they were told that it was possible to locate the witness and to contact him, therefore to question him. But you said that you had failed to do so without specifying why. So I would like you to return to the question to address the reason why you did not contact the witness, because you seem to say that after all he was a crucial witness for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: There may be a problem in interpretation. During the course of the trial the Prosecution had been in contact with both the witnesses, had interviewed them, had taken statements from them. But when it came time for them to come to court or came time for them to testify, in the case of Mr. Kabashi, they were unwilling. What I was speaking of - and this may have caused the confusion - was the efforts made in anticipation of this appeal by the Prosecution to confirm, at the very least, that the witnesses were still alive and could be contacted in the event that a re-trial was ordered. I have said in -- that we made formal requests to both countries. One of the countries has informally replied that the witness is alive. The second country has not replied informally, other than to say that, "We are looking into the request and we will get back to you hopefully before the hearing." And I called them last night asking for an informal update and I have not received one. It's not that we aren't making efforts to inquire as to whether the witnesses are available in the loose sense. In terms of the question why I have not gone to interview the witnesses or attempt to interview them, I didn't think it was appropriate at this occasion to put the witnesses through the pain of an interview which may be for naught. We will certainly communicate with the witnesses directly if there is an order for re-trial; that you can rest assured. Might I continue, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you. These witnesses were successfully intimidated. They refused to testify on the merits of the case, notwithstanding the prospect of being prosecuted for contempt. The Trial Chamber proceeded to judgement, as I've said, without their credible, relevant, and probative evidence. In its management of the trial, the Trial Chamber abused its discretion when it failed to receive their evidence before declaring the Prosecution case closed. As we point out in detail in our brief, a review of the transcript from October and November of 2007 demonstrates that the Trial Chamber was so intent on achieving an expeditious trial that it lost its way to ensuring that the trial was also fair. I want to pause briefly here to emphasise that the Prosecution accepts that an expeditious trial can be fair. However, we argue - as occurred in this case - that when witness intimidation becomes a prominent feature in a trial, an expeditious trial may become unfair if the Trial Chamber does not properly deal with the consequences of witness intimidation. Not since the Tadic appeal judgement has fair trial under Article 20 been so central to an appeal. The basic principle is found in Tadic appeal judgement at paragraph 43: "The right to a fair trial is central to the rule of law; it upholds the due process of law." In the Tadic appeal, the Defence experienced difficulties in obtaining evidence because of lack of cooperation from authorities in Republika Srpska. In this appeal, the evidence was unavailable because Prosecution witnesses were intimidated and fearful of giving testimony. To my knowledge, this is the first time witness intimidation will be specifically addressed on appeal as an issue under Article 20(1). Your Honours may recall the words in paragraph 55 of the Tadic appeal judgement where it was stated that: "The Appeals Chamber can conceive of situations where a fair trial is not possible because witnesses central to the Defence case do not appear due to obstructionist efforts of a State." In this appeal, the Prosecution notes that witnesses central to the case against the accused did not appear due to intimidation and other obstructionist efforts. This created a situation similar to that forecast in the Tadic appeals judgement; a situation where a fair trial was not possible. Only in this case, the affected party was the Prosecution, not the Defence. In the Jelesic appeals judgement Your Honours decided that Article 20 applies to the Prosecution's participation as one of the parties to the trial. At paragraph 27 Your Honours said: "Failure to hear a party against whom the Trial Chamber is provisionally inclined is not consistent with the requirement to hold a fair trial ... the availability of this right to the Prosecution and its exercise of the right can be of importance to the making of a correct decision by the Trial Chamber." The Prosecution was also the aggrieved party in the Prosecutor versus Nahimana, and I refer Your Honours to the ICTR appeal judgement at paragraph 173. Should you need more reference that the Prosecution is entitled to a fair trial, I also refer you to the Milutinovic decision denying Prosecution's request for certification of Rule 73 bis issue for appeal dated 30 August 2006. At paragraph 10 the Trial Chamber held that: "Although use of the word 'fairness' in the context of a criminal trial might commonly refer to fairness for an accused, the Prosecution undoubtedly is entitled to a fair opportunity to present its case. The Statute of the Tribunal obligates each Trial Chamber to 'ensure that the trial is fair and expeditious ... with ... respect for the rights of the accused,' and does not provide that only an accused is entitled to be treated equitably." Since you're citing Article 20(1), I note that you referred to the rights of the accused. What do you say about the apparent hierarchy that is established by the article favouring "full respect for the rights of the accused and due regard ..." which appears to be at a lower level "for the protection of victims and witnesses"? While it is acknowledged that the Trial Chamber has a duty to ensure a fair and expeditious trial and while it is acknowledged that the Prosecution is entitled to fairness, it cannot be at the expense of the requirement to ensure full respect for the rights of the accused. And it may very well be that the Trial Chamber felt it had gone sufficiently far in ensuring due regard for the protection of the witnesses and that it was of the view that had it gone any further it would be breaching the obligation to ensure full respect for the rights of the accused. Simple answer to that question is that the primary obligation is to do two things: To have a fair trial and to have an expeditious trial. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you can't ignore the rest of the paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'm not ignoring the rights of the accused, Your Honour. The rights of the accused were assiduously respected in this case. The witnesses were not protected fully. Many were intimidated, many were threatened, and as the words of some of the witnesses suggest, others were killed. The assessment of whether the trial was fair takes into account all of these issues, and our position is that when witness intimidation becomes so serious that the Trial Chamber's protective measures and other steps become inadequate and are unable to ensure that evidence that is relevant and probative is heard and received or received, then the trial becomes unfair --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I don't know if I can say it too many times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Our position, I think, is clear, simple. And I fully understand Your Honours' concerns about the rights of the accused, but this Chamber and this Tribunal has taken into account extraordinary situations to craft rules and to craft decisions to ensure that relevant evidence is received in circumstances where it has been made impossible for a variety of reasons, and I refer to 92 quater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, you told me earlier that the Prosecution itself did not make any specific submission for the reception of the evidence of these two witnesses under 89(F).

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Isn't that astonishing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: We made an application for Mr. Kabashi -- for his evidence to be received under 92 quater and the Trial Chamber quite simply said: It doesn't fit the mold, and that was the end of the story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But not 89(F).

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: We had not made the application under 89 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're making that for the first time here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I am raising that as an opportunity for this Appeals Chamber to deal with the serious problem, to give guidance to the Trial Chambers when this problem comes again, as it is in other cases, and to give them the guidance as to how they should think about creating a fair trial, where witness intimidation works hard to prevent one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you say that it fell to the Trial Chamber in its discharge of its fundamental obligation to ensure the fairness of the trial to have itself proprio motu receive this evidence under 89(F)?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: There was nothing preventing the Trial Chamber from doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, continue, Mr. Kremer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can just check the time so I can ensure that my colleague has ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: In this case, the Prosecution brought examples of witness intimidation to the Trial Chamber's attention as they were reported to it. This information helped secure protective measures for large number of witnesses. Protective measures assisted the Prosecution witnesses to testify viva voce. The Trial Chamber described the scope of the problem it faced as "a high proportion of Prosecution witnesses in this case expressed fear of appearing before the Trial Chamber to give evidence." This fear was for their personal safety and the safety of their families. In 34 cases the Trial Chamber granted protective measures. It accepted fear as an objectively well-grounded risk to the security and welfare of the witness or the witness's family should it become known that the witness had given evidence before the Tribunal. I refer you to trial judgement paragraph 22. As mentioned in paragraph 6 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber granted protective measures to witnesses who appeared before it. However, the Trial Chamber itself accepted that its protective measures alone could not ensure the receipt of all of the evidence in the face of witness intimidation. At paragraph 28, the Trial Chamber admitted "a few witnesses who were expected to give evidence on central aspects of the case were never heard." As the Tadic appeals judgement observed at paragraph 55: "The obligation is on the complaining party to bring the difficulties to the attention of the Trial Chamber forthwith so that the latter," that is, the Trial Chamber, "can determine whether any assistance could be provided under the Rules or Statute to relieve the situation. The party cannot remain silent on the matter only to return on appeal to seek a trial de novo, as the Defence seeks to do in this case." Our submission is that the Prosecution has met this obligation. It has brought the problem of witness intimidation to the Chamber's attention, and given the massive notice -- or the notice of massive witness intimidation, the Trial Chamber had a responsibility to address the problem and to find a solution. What was required was a vigorous approach to ensure a fair trial. In Prosecution -- Prosecutor versus Goran Jelesic at paragraph 16 the Appeals Chamber observed as follows: "... in long and complicated cases, such as most of those which come to the Tribunal, it is necessary for the Trial Chamber to exercise control over the proceedings. That control may well need to be vigorous provided of course that it does not encroach on the right of a party to a fair hearing." The Chamber's discussion at paragraphs 22 to 28 about how it dealt with the many intimidated witnesses does not meet the Jelesic test. The Trial Chamber's discussion does not answer its failure to receive critical evidence, does not answer its failure to search for the truth, and does not answer its failure to do justice to the victims and the international community. In paragraph 28, the Trial Chamber suggested that it "made use of all its powers under the Rules to facilitate the reception of evidence without stepping beyond its role as an impartial finder of facts." However, this opinion does not excuse the Trial Chamber from not fulfilling its guiding statutory duty, the duty to ensure a fair trial. What should the Trial Chamber have done to discharge its duty to ensure a fair trial when confronted with massive witness intimidation during the trial? As we say, it should have followed the Jelesic guidance and exercised the necessary vigorous control over the trial proceedings to ensure that the evidence -- of crucial evidence was received despite the campaign of intimidation. In this case, a fair trial became impossible when the Trial Chamber denied itself the opportunity to receive critical evidence from these two witnesses who had been intimidated and refused to testify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, let me be clear about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The only failure of which you accuse the Trial Chamber is not receiving the evidence under 89(F). Is there anything else that you are saying that the Trial Chamber should have done?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: In our brief we also point out the fact that they could have deferred the conclusion of the Prosecution's case until further efforts were made to have the two witnesses testify. They closed it off on the 20th of November with -- without following the rest of the steps in respect of Shefqet Kabashi, and they took no further steps -- in fact, closed the case on the 26th of November with respect to the other witness. So it was clear that at that time the Prosecution case was closed and the Trial Chamber was having no more part in its efforts to try and have these witnesses testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So those are the two things --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Basically, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- for which you -- don't say "basically." I want to be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Those are the two things for which you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- blame the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- Trial Chamber? Considering that the proceedings are, at the base, adversarial, I mean isn't it, as I said before, astonishing that the Prosecution did not ask for the reception of the evidence under 89(F)?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I can only confirm that it -- that the motion was never made. I won't say more. But our position is that if a fair trial doesn't result, then -- because of the witness intimidation that had been squarely before the Trial Chamber from the beginning, a motion shouldn't matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Indeed, in the absence of the Prosecution not making that specific submission, you really don't know, you're not in a position to say, that the Trial Chamber didn't consider 89(F). The Trial Chamber might very well have considered 89(F) and concluded that it wasn't worth the while.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: It doesn't appear anywhere in the judgement, so one can only speculate; and hopefully Your Honours won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Pocar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: On this point, in paragraph 28 of the judgement, the trial judgement, in concluding the chapter on difficulties of obtaining witness testimony, the Trial Chamber concludes that it made use of all its powers under the Rules to facilitate the reception of evidence without stepping beyond its role as an impartial finder of facts. Is that your position that had the Trial Chamber made use of 89(F) would not have stepped beyond its role as an impartial finder of fact or -- but let me put it like that: Do you interpret this as the Chamber having said that maybe admitting proprio motu evidence would have brought the Chamber to step beyond its role as an impartial finder of fact. So perhaps the Chamber might have considered the point, but came to the conclusion that doing -- intervening more in the absence of a specific request of the Prosecution would have put in danger its position as -- of impartiality in finding the facts? What is your ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: If one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So there is some reasoning made by the Chamber on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: The statement made by the Chamber is explained by what appears in the earlier parts of the judgement which show the Rules and the procedures it applied to receive evidence. It did not refer to Rule 89(F) as a vehicle through which it received evidence during the course of the case. And at paragraph 28 it says that "... the Chamber made use of all its powers under the Rules to facilitate," and when one looks at the powers it applied, it didn't apply 89(F) without stepping beyond its role as an impartial finder of facts. Our position is that they could have applied -- the Trial Chamber could have applied Rule 89(F) without stepping beyond its role as an impartial finder of facts if it had given the proper cautions to itself as to how this evidence could be used so as not to prejudice the rights of the Defence. And that -- I think the guidance from that comes in part from 92 quater and the use of statements of witnesses that are not cross-examined on has been dealt with thoroughly by this Chamber in the Haraqija and Morina decision or judgement that came out not too long ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Meron, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Kremer, you are presenting an argument which is a very difficult one to make. In answering my previous question you explained that the evidence under 89(F), had it been presented, the statement, would have made a real difference, and yet the Prosecution did not make a motion on that, they are making this argument for the first time in the Appeals Chamber and in the brief to the Appeals Chamber. It's very, very difficult to be sympathetic to an argument which raised the matter of - as you are saying - of such great importance and the Prosecutor slept on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I hear you. The appeal brief and the notice of appeal looked at the judgement, and the result of the judgement and our position was clearly there was not a fair trial because these witnesses were never heard. And the Trial Chamber didn't do enough to try to hear these witnesses. In preparing for this appeal, it also occurred to me that the Trial Chamber could have and should have asked itself the question as to whether this evidence could have been received in another way because it had the obligation to ensure that the trial was fair. Our position is that without the evidence of these witnesses the trial could never be fair. And if there's another vehicle it could have looked at, I offer that as a vehicle. I also offer it as an opportunity for this Court to give guidance to Trial Chambers as to what to do in these circumstances where witness intimidation is causing witnesses not to testify or not to come to court and their intimidation is provable, where it's real, where the witnesses are saying, "I'm afraid to testify because my family's been threatened or because I've been threatened or people I know have been killed," and so on. So it is -- I view this case in part as an opportunity for the law to move forward on issues that, up until this point, have not been relevant on an appeal, and it is something that I suggest is very worthwhile to consider seriously and to give some direction on, regardless of what the result of this appeal is. If I could just have a moment to see the notes I've just been passed. I'm reminded in respect of the other efforts we made with respect to Mr. Kabashi and the entering of his statements, we also tried to call the investigator to provide hearsay evidence as to the statements that he had provided to the OTP, and that was refused as well. So short of asking under 89(F), we tried every other procedure that was at least considered at the time to have the testimony of Mr. Kabashi received. The Trial Chamber was not sympathetic and no attempts thus were made to have the evidence of the second witness -- using the same motions because it was clear that they would be refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: If the Registrar could tell me how much time I have left, I may just summarise my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yeah, he just passed me a note. You have used one hour and three minutes and you are allotted an hour and a - what is it? - 20 minutes. So you have 17 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to close my submissions with -- and I think I've been a little bit repetitive on the point, but I can't stress enough with what I've just said that the Trial Chamber had an opportunity to ensure that the trial was fair by taking greater steps to have these witnesses heard or their evidence received. It did not achieve that and our position is, with respect, that the Appeals Chamber should acknowledge the fact that the trial was unfair and refer the matter back for a re-trial. If Your Honours can be assisted by a more detailed delineation as to which parts of the statements are relevant to the various counts, we're certainly prepared to provide that and the Defence can provide a response if that would be helpful, as Judge Vaz has asked. I don't have time, unfortunately, to go through that because I think it would be unfair to the -- to Your Honours not to hear from my colleague on ground three because I believe - and our submission is - that it's an important ground that bears proper consideration. So subject to any questions that you may have after her remarks are concluded that I haven't yet answered, I'm certainly prepared to address them and hopefully to the extent that there is anything that arises out of the Defence remarks that I can be helpful with, I will do that during my reply. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kremer. We are about five minutes from the break and we're going to take the break for about half an hour. So we return half an hour from now. You can work out the maths. And then we'll hear from Mr. Emmerson. We're adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll continue with the Prosecution. It's now the turn of Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARTIN SALGADO
utterances.text: Martin Salgado. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Salgado. You have about 15, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARTIN SALGADO
utterances.text: Thank you. Under the Prosecution's third ground of appeal, we argue that the Chamber erred in fact with respect to Witness 61 and erred in law with respect to Witness 1. Today I will focus on the error of fact, but before I begin I would just like to tell you that Witness 61, who is the rape victim, is a woman, whilst Witness 1 is a man. But given the similarity of the victims' pseudonyms and given that Witness 61 is the only woman I need to mention, I will refer to her as the woman or by using the feminine. No reasonable Trial Chamber could fail to conclude that the woman's rapist was Idriz Balaj. Five armed men came to the house where she and Witness 1 were staying. They came around midnight and they wore black uniforms with KLA insignia. Among them was a man called Toger. The woman testified that Toger came inside the house. She heard the other four soldiers call him Toger. "Toger" means lieutenant in Albanian. The armed men took the witnesses together to a house they knew as the KLA headquarters in Rznic and once then there the witnesses were separated. Two of the soldiers put Witness 1 in a well where he was left standing with water up to his waist. The woman gave evidence that two of the other soldiers took her directly to a room in the house, whilst Witness 1 stated that Toger took her to the house. Witness 1 recognised Toger because he knew him from before. The woman was then left alone in the room with the soldier she knew as Toger. Toger interrogated her about whether her husband had collaborated with the Serbian police. Toger then raped her several times. After the rape, Toger told the woman to leave the room. Her husband was then brought in to be interrogated, and you can find that at transcript page 3996, 4024, 4025, 4045 [realtime transcript read in error "4046"]. Soon after being released she told her husband and other relatives that Toger had raped her, and they reported the rape that same morning to the local KLA. As shown from these facts, she identified her rapist as the KLA soldier called Toger. The Chamber found that Toger is Idriz Balaj, and in light of this finding it was unreasonable to acquit Balaj of rape. In finding doubt as to whether Toger or another KLA soldier raped her, the Chamber made three consecutive errors which can be found in paragraph 469 of the judgement. First, the Chamber misinterpreted her evidence, finding that she might have confused Toger with someone else because it was too dark to see the soldiers who came to her house. Second, the Chamber mistakenly found that Witness 1's inability to see who brought the woman into the room where she was raped raised doubt about the rapist's identity. And third, the Chamber placed undue emphasis on the woman's recollection of her rapist's physical appearance, finding that it raised doubt about his identity. And it was the compounding effect of these three errors that led the Chamber to the wrong conclusion of finding doubt where none was reasonable. I will deal very briefly with each. The Chamber misinterpreted the woman's evidence. It found that it is "possible" that she confused Toger with someone else because "she testified that it was too dark for her to see the soldiers who came to her house." This error is rooted in the Chamber's incorrect summary of her evidence at paragraph 460 of the judgement. The Chamber relied on transcript page 4043 to find that darkness prevented her from describing the soldiers. However, transcript page 4043 referred to the three soldiers she saw outside her home, not to Toger who went inside the house. She testified that Toger came inside her house and she saw him there. She also heard the other soldiers refer to him as Toger, and that's at transcript page 4005 and at transcript page 4001. She only knew one person as Toger. She identified Toger as the soldier who interrogated and raped her. The Chamber accepted her evidence that one of the men was addressed as Toger by the others, and in light of this the finding that she might have confused Toger with someone else was unreasonable. The Chamber's second error was to find reasonable doubt based on Witness 1's inability to see who brought the woman into the room where she was raped. Witness 1 never gave evidence as to who brought the woman into the room. He gave evidence as to who brought her to the house. The only first-hand evidence of what went on in the room was the woman's clear and consistent testimony that she was raped by Toger. The fact that Witness 1 did not see who took the woman into the room cannot detract from the woman's clear evidence and does not raise doubt, and the Chamber was unreasonable to find otherwise. The woman testified that when she was separated from Witness 1, she was taken directly to a room and left there alone with Toger. There was one soldier, one of the soldiers who had taken her from her home, who stayed at the door, but Toger told him to leave. She was then left alone in the room with Toger, and after interrogating her Toger raped her repeatedly. In addition and relevant to this second error, the woman contemporaneously communicated that Toger had raped her, and that is the evidence of Witness 1 and also at transcript pages 4048 and transcript pages 7108 and 7109. And on the strength of this communication her relatives then complained that same morning to the local KLA leaders about Toger raping the woman. Turning to the third error, the Chamber found that the woman's recollection of her rapist's physical appearance was insufficient or did not fit Balaj, but it was unreasonable to conclude that this finding created doubt about Balaj's responsibility. Again, she heard her rapist being referred to as Toger and she contemporaneously identified the man who raped her as Toger. And this evidence is not undermined by her later failure to recognise Balaj in a photo-board four years after the rape or by her courtroom testimony nine years after the rape that she would no longer recognise the rapist. Also, her clear and consistent evidence that Toger raped her is not undermined by her observation that when she saw Balaj on television in The Hague, he did not look like Toger but looked older. This observation was made seven years after the rape. It is not surprising that Balaj looked older than her rapist did at the time. When describing Toger, the woman mentioned six features, you can find four of them summarised at paragraph 460 of the judgement. All of these features are consistent with Balaj. The six features are: Origin, she mentioned that he was not from her village and Toger -- excuse me, Balaj is from a different municipality altogether; age, she said Toger was in his mid-20s and Balaj would at the time have been 26 or 27; language; hair colour; height, she described Toger as a little taller than her, and that's at transcript page 4000, Balaj is 20 centimetres taller than the witness, but this is not a material difference because since what amounts to a little is subjective and what is material is that Balaj is taller, not shorter, than the witness; and the final feature: Command. Her evidence shows that Toger acted as the person in authority the night she was raped. He acted like someone with authority over the men who accompanied him. He asked them to bring him a wooden stick and ordered them to leave from the room. He acted as the person with authority over the witness when he interrogated her and when he told her to go to the bed and to get undressed and also when after the rape he told her not to tell her husband and to leave the room. Toger was in command during the events that night, and the Chamber failed to consider this as an identifying characteristic of the rapist. And this feature additionally denotes that the KLA soldier she called Toger was Balaj. The Chamber found under a different incident that "Toger" means "lieutenant" in Albanian. It found that there was only one Toger in the Dukagjin area during the indictment period. It found that the evidence was consistent with Balaj holding a position of authority within the KLA and wearing a black uniform, just like the man who came to the witness's home. In addition to these findings, the evidence showed that Balaj was in command of the Black Eagles, and this was a KLA unit that was stationed in the house where the witnesses were taken to and where Witness 61 was raped. And we have set out our evidence to that effect in paragraph 53 of our appeal brief. To conclude on the factual error, Witness 61, the woman, was the victim of rape and torture. And during her rape she was so afraid that the rapist would kill her that she dare not scream and for three years after the rape she was unable to bear children and needed treatment. And notwithstanding these traumatic circumstances, her evidence was consistent that it was Toger who raped her. Having accepted her evidence that one of the men was addressed as Toger and having found that Balaj is Toger, the Chamber unreasonably failed to convict Balaj. And the Appeals Chamber should correct this injustice and find Idriz Balaj guilty of her rape, her torture, and cruel treatment, and sentence him accordingly. If I may just say two things about the error of law that I haven't gone into. It's our submission that in failing to find that Witness 1 was cruelly treated, the Chamber erred in law because it failed to subsume the factual findings it made under the correct statutory provision. What the Appeals Chamber should do is apply the correct law to these factual findings and find that Witness 1 was cruelly treated in relation to the entire conduct as found by the Chamber, and this conduct was not limited to putting Witness 1 in a well but extended to the whole conduct charge. The second thing is because of its legal error, the Chamber did not make any findings on Balaj's responsibility for committing cruel treatment against Witness 1, but in our submission Balaj, together with other MLA [sic] soldiers, personally participated in the acts amounting to cruel treatment, including by interrogating Witness 1. In a different case the Limaj Trial Chamber convicted an accused at paragraph 652 of the judgement of committing the crime of cruel treatment together with others. It found he personally participated in the material elements of the crime, and on this basis the Appeals Chamber should find that Balaj, together with other KLA soldiers, participated in the conduct amounting to cruel treatment and sentence him accordingly. Thank you. Unless you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Ms. Salgado.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARTIN SALGADO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's now for Mr. Emmerson -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Just a very brief one. Is statement of Kabashi in appendix A to the appeals brief, the statement to which Mr. Kremer referred to before under 89(F) --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question. Appendix A to your appeals brief --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: -- contains the statement by Kabashi -- statements by Kabashi of 24 October 2004 and 1 June 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Is this -- is one of these statements the statement you referred to before --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes, the October 24th, 2004, statement was not included in the original filing and it was corrected by way of an addendum to that filing I believe shortly after the filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So when you referred to the Trial Chamber's not admitting things under 89(F) --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, members of the Appeals Chamber, the submissions I make on behalf of Mr. Haradinaj are confined to ground one. Put shortly, we say that the Prosecution's arguments on this ground are fundamentally misconceived. Their submissions are factually selective and wholly underestimate the lengths to which the Trial Chamber went in

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: say that the Prosecution has not come anywhere near establishing that the Trial Chamber committed a discernible error or abused its discretion. Moreover, and perhaps more fundamentally, we respectfully submit that the Prosecution's conception of what constitutes a fair trial is wrong. For Mr. Kremer to suggest that this trial could never be fair, as he said, without the evidence of these two witnesses is, in our submission, simply to misconstrue the requirements of a fair trial. What the Statute and the Rules together require is that a fair trial is a trial which is conducted fairly and in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and with full respect to those Rules which are aimed at the protection of the rights of the accused. Mr. President, on a proper analysis of the facts, it is, we say, quite clear that the Trial Chamber provided the Prosecution with an entirely adequate and reasonable opportunity to obtain the testimony of these two witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
