utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we say that on a proper analysis of the facts it is quite clear that the Trial Chamber provided the Prosecution with an entirely fair and reasonable opportunity to obtain and present the testimony of these two witnesses. Both of the witnesses maintained a staunch refusal to testify throughout the trial in the full knowledge of the potential consequences of their actions and with the benefit of legal advice. The Trial Chamber made strenuous and repeated attempts to obtain their testimony and to compel them to give evidence, and when they refused to testify voluntarily in The Hague the Trial Chamber granted Prosecution requests for subpoenas and compelled videolink testimony from the witnesses' places of residence outside of Kosovo. It set aside two sitting dates for Shefqet Kabashi and three for the other witness. It made requests for assistance to the relevant states. It initiated contempt proceedings in the case of Shefqet Kabashi, and it permitted the Prosecution to extend its case beyond the time which had been allocated to it on three separate occasions in an effort to enable the Prosecution to call the evidence of these witnesses. To use a colloquialism, the Trial Chamber bent over backwards to secure their testimony. By the end of the Prosecution's case, there was no realistic prospect that either witness would change his position and agree to testify. Having regard to the steps which had already been taken and in the absence of any indication that either witness would be prepared to testify at any foreseeable time in the future, the Trial Chamber was, we say, fully entitled to take the view that the Prosecution had been afforded a fair and reasonable opportunity to present its case and we invite the Appeals Chamber to endorse that conclusion. In essence, and as it boils down in the submissions of Mr. Kremer, there are two central complaints being put forward and may I deal with them in reverse order. The first appears to be that the Trial Chamber did not of its own motion admit the statements under Rule 89(F) in the absence of any application by the Prosecution. The second and more general submission is the one which the Prosecution made in their appeals brief, namely, that the Trial Chamber should have allowed more time and made more efforts within the Rules as they were currently being applied on the facts of this case. I say that is the point made in their appeals brief because the argument that Mr. Kremer has advanced before you this morning, which the Prosecution say was so obvious and so clearly a requirement of fairness that the Trial Chamber should have taken the point of its own motion, was not only not taken at trial but it wasn't taken by the Prosecution in their appeal brief to this Court either. It is, in other words, an afterthought. Since the details are potentially important, it's inevitable that I'll have to go into the history of the proceedings in just a little depth on certain points, but before I do that I want to say, if I may, a word or two at the outset about the overall length of time that the Trial Chamber allocated to the Prosecution to present its case. Because in the Prosecution's appeal brief it is suggested that that allowance was insufficient and is evidence that this Trial Chamber was elevating expedition above fairness. The basic position is this: At the Pre-Trial Conference on the 1st of March, the Prosecution was allocated 125 hours to present its evidence in chief. The OTP senior trial attorney, Mr. David Re, made no suggestion at that time or thereafter that this was insufficient to do justice to the Prosecution case, nor did the Prosecution at any stage apply to the Trial Chamber for an increase in the number of hours that had been allocated to it, and the Registry records show that the Prosecution used about 128 hours in calling Prosecution witnesses in chief. Why does any of this matter? Mr. President, for the purposes of this appeal we respectfully submit that the overall time allocated to the Prosecution is of little if any relevance at all. I say this because the Trial Chamber made it quite clear in its successive rulings on each of these two witnesses that it was prepared to allow the Prosecution to exceed the time that had been allocated to it if only the Prosecution was in a position to demonstrate that either of the two witnesses would be willing to testify. The decisive reason why neither of them gave evidence in the end wasn't because the Prosecution had exceeded the time that the Trial Chamber allowed to it, but because both of the witnesses resolutely and repeatedly refused to testify and because that still remained their position until the very end of the proceedings. Shefqet Kabashi, as Mr. Kremer pointed out, was first called by the Prosecution on the 5th of June. After taking the solemn declaration, he then refused to answer any questions put to him by the Prosecution. Contrary to the selective impression that was given by the Prosecution, both in their written brief and in Mr. Kremer's submissions, he did not say that the reason why he was refusing to testify was because he was afraid; indeed, he said quite the contrary. It's fair to say that reading the record as a whole he gave a number of different explanations for his refusal which were inconsistent and, to some extent, incoherent. It's right as you heard at one point he said he could only comply with his civic duty to testify within the framework of a normal life which does not exist, he said, in Kosovo. But he went on to state categorically that no one had threatened him and no one had forced him not to testify and in terms that his refusal to give evidence was not because of fear. Indeed, he made some specified and some particularised allegations of intimidation against the Prosecution rather than against the Defence, and said that in the light of these he was unable to testify morally or psychologically. The Presiding Judge repeatedly warned him that he was under a duty to testify and that if he maintained his refusal he would be liable to be held in contempt of the Tribunal and would be liable to be sentenced of up to seven years' imprisonment. Mr. Kabashi for his part made it clear that he understood the consequences of not testifying and he said that he was willing to go to prison for contempt rather than to testify. He was provided with experienced legal counsel from the Tribunal, Mr. Michael Karnavas, to ensure that he fully understood his position and to make representations on his behalf. And after giving Mr. Kabashi an opportunity to consult with Mr. Karnavas, the Presiding Judge again asked him to confirm that he understood the consequences of his maintaining his refusal to testify, Mr. Kabashi said that he did, and this was confirmed by Mr. Karnavas. So the Trial Chamber then moved to the next stage provided for under the Rules, it decided to prosecute Mr. Kabashi for contempt and issued an order in lieu of indictment under Rule 77(D). He was summoned to appear before the Trial Chamber on the 7th of June. He failed to attend and instead returned to his country of residence without authorisation, whereupon the Trial Chamber moved to the next stage provided by the Rules. It issued an arrest warrant and an order for Mr. Kabashi's surrender to the competent authorities of the United States, requesting them to arrest him and hand him over to the custody of the ICTY. Now, as a result of inquiries made by the Registry, the Trial Chamber suspended the arrest warrant on the 4th of July, and this was because the Registry had been informed by the US embassy in The Hague that Mr. Kabashi had changed his mind and agreed to travel voluntarily to The Hague, but when the Registry made direct contact with Mr. Kabashi to make the necessary travel arrangements he told them that he wasn't prepared to come. And so the Trial Chamber did the next logical thing and re-instated the arrest warrant. Despite a series of further attempts by the Trial Chamber to arrange for Mr. Kabashi's arrest and surrender by the United States authorities, he never returned to the seat of the Tribunal to appear in his contempt case, and in all of his communications with the Registry he steadfastly maintained a refusal to testify. The Prosecution, for its part, took no steps at all after his refusal on the 5th of June to give evidence to secure his testimony until the 25th of October, just 12 days before its case was scheduled to end. And on that day and for the first time it applied for an order compelling Mr. Kabashi to testify via videolink from the United States. The Trial Chamber indicated that it was minded to grant that application because all other attempts had failed to secure his testimony, and in order to facilitate the videolink the Trial Chamber twice granted the Prosecution's requests to extend the date for the close of its case in order to hear the videolink. In other words, the Trial Chamber made it perfectly clear that it wasn't going to elevate form over substance and was going to provide the Prosecution with whatever opportunities it could reasonably do without imposing a time guillotine if the Prosecution could show the witness would come forward and would testify. So Mr. Kabashi appeared via videolink on the 20th of November, together with his defence counsel from the Federal Republic Defenders' Office in the Federal Court from the southern district of New York, a man called Mr. Davidson, who had been appointed for the specific purpose of advising and representing Mr. Kabashi in the contempt proceedings which were part of this Court's enforcement procedure in an effort to obtain his testimony. He was also represented at this end of the videolink by Mr. Karnavas, his Tribunal-appointed lawyer. And as soon as the hearing began Mr. Kabashi indicated that he was not prepared to testify and Mr. Davidson confirmed this. So this was the second opportunity, videolink established, he is there in the courtroom, and he is refusing at that stage to testify. Choosing his words with care - and the Prosecution seem to fasten on this but, with respect, it's plainly obvious what was going on - choosing his words with care, Mr. Davidson said that Mr. Kabashi was not prepared to testify that day, although this was without prejudice to any decision he might make in the future, and the Prosecution say that indicates Mr. Kabashi was in dialogue with the Tribunal. Well, with the greatest of respect the qualification that was entered by his counsel but not by Mr. Kabashi himself, you may think, was no doubt entered to lay foundation for any defence Mr. Kabashi might advance in contempt proceedings in the United States rather than to evidence any sincere intention to change his position and to testify. The Trial Chamber nonetheless insisted that he should take the solemn declaration, which he did. He then once again refused to answer any question put to him by the Prosecution. The Prosecution was permitted to consult directly with Mr. Davidson via videolink to New York and with Mr. Karnavas at the same time in order to explain through them to Mr. Kabashi that if he changed his position and agreed to testify then the contempt indictment against him was likely to be discharged, but when the videolink resumed, despite this opportunity having been provided, Mr. Kabashi again confirmed that he was still not prepared to testify and both Mr. Davidson and Mr. Karnavas also confirmed this. At that point the Prosecution sought a further adjournment in the hearing, and Judge Orie pointed out that we had reached a stage whereby the Trial Chamber had been struggling to secure Mr. Kabashi's testimony for many months and that he had repeatedly refused to testify, that he had at one stage said he would come back voluntarily and had then refused to do so. Judge Orie said that if, despite all this, there were to be a dramatic change in Mr. Kabashi's attitude which gave cause to believe he genuinely did intend to testify, then the Trial Chamber would entertain any application the Prosecution wish to make in order to enable it to receive his testimony, but Judge Orie warned that the Trial Chamber would not engage in what he called an endless continuing story with this witness. It's a story which, in fact, is being continued through ground one in this appeal. After the hearing, the Prosecution wrote to Mr. Davidson in an effort to persuade him -- I'm sorry, in an effort to persuade Mr. Kabashi through Mr. Davidson to change his mind, but the plain fact is that he never did change his mind. Despite this, the Prosecution made three subsequent applications, each of which was in the circumstances inevitably doomed to failure. The first was made on the 23rd of November. The Prosecution filed a motion to extend its case on the ground that there was a real possibility that Mr. Kabashi might change his mind if he was given yet further legal advice. The Prosecution was not then, however, able to point to any change of circumstances. There was no indication that Mr. Kabashi had changed his mind, nor was there any indication from either of his lawyers that his position was liable to change. It was a purely speculative application and it was rejected, quite rightly, by the Trial Chamber three days later on the grounds that there had change in circumstances since Mr. Kabashi's final refusal to testify during the last videolink. The Prosecution indeed conceded in its application that Mr. Kabashi was still, at the time that they were applying to extend their case was again, unwilling to testify. So, said the Trial Chamber, the mere possibility that he might change his mind at some unspecified point in the future if he got further legal advice wasn't a sufficient justification to continue extending the Prosecution case. The Chamber had said quite clearly, recorded in its judgement, that it would consider receiving his testimony if there was a dramatic change in his attitude and if there was cause to believe that he would actually give evidence but nothing of that kind had happened. And as for a possible change in the light of legal advice, the Chamber pointed out in its ruling that Mr. Kabashi had received competent legal advice not just from one lawyer but from two on the consequences of his actions from the beginning but had maintained throughout his refusal to testify. Mr. President, we respectfully submit that the Trial Chamber was entirely justified in reaching that conclusion. And Mr. Kabashi's position had remained constant for over five and a half months, and there was no indication of any change to his position in the foreseeable future. From the outset he'd been made fully aware of the potential penal consequences of his actions, and he'd received competent legal advice from experienced counsel. The Prosecution had already been afforded two separate opportunities to obtain his testimony and had, by that time, provided both of his legal advisors with all of the information the Prosecution wanted to put before them in order to advise their clients not only once but twice. The Trial Chamber had then allowed the Prosecution twice to extend its case and it was, in our submission, entirely appropriate for it to draw a line and to refuse the Prosecution what amounted to a third indefinite and unspecified adjournment to its case at the end of its case in the speculative hope and with no basis whatever that Mr. Kabashi might change his mind. The Prosecution's next application was as doomed as its last. After the case was closed and after the Trial Chamber had issued its Scheduling Order for the filing of final briefs and closing arguments, on the 30th of November the Prosecution re-filed a request for certification. The Trial Chamber refused the request and they refused it on the basis that it didn't raise an issue which could significantly affect the outcome of the trial. Why could it not significantly affect the outcome of the trial? The answer, in the Trial Chamber's view, was that even if they had extended the case Mr. Kabashi would still not be giving evidence because his position was demonstrably consistent and to accede to the Prosecution's application would, in effect, have required the Trial Chamber to keep the Prosecution's case open indefinitely with no indication of any grounds for doing so. And again, we say that the Trial Chamber plainly was right and correctly applied the provisions of Rule 73(B). The Prosecution hadn't shown and has not shown that the Trial Judges committed any discernible error. Finally, on the 17th of December the Prosecution applied for an order permitting it to re-open its case and for a judicial representation to be made to the US authorities. Now, just putting that application in context. By that time that application was made the evidence had been closed for more than two weeks and the parties were engaged in drafting final briefs. What the Prosecution sought was an order that they should be permitted to call Mr. Kabashi to testify if they could secure his evidence at any time before the filing of closing briefs on the 14th of January, 2008, but once again the application was made without any indication that there had been a material change of circumstances. The Prosecution didn't suggest that Mr. Kabashi was willing to testify or that there had been any indication that he was likely to change his mind in the foreseeable future. Mr. President, members of the Appeals Chamber, you will recall from the brief and the documents with it that the application was based on comments made by a district judge in judicial proceedings in the United States which had been instituted against Mr. Kabashi for contempt in respect of his failure to answer questions during the videolink. And the judge had held that under federal law he could not hold Mr. Kabashi in contempt because at the time the contempt application was made there were no extant proceedings in this Tribunal, and civil contempt under federal law could only be used as a means of coercing a person to testify in ongoing proceedings and so, said the district judge, there were no ongoing proceedings in which his evidence could be coerced, but in an aside he observed that if the Trial Chamber were to re-open the evidence and set a specific date for Mr. Kabashi to testify, then in those circumstances he would in all likelihood issue an order compelling him to do so, but he wasn't prepared to make an order in those proceedings because the possibility that the evidence might be re-opened was nothing more than theoretical. And it was on the basis of those comments that the Prosecution again applied to the Trial Chamber at that very late stage in the proceedings to re-open the evidence and set a date for Mr. Kabashi to testify with no indication whatever that he would give evidence if such a date was set. And on the 23rd of December, the Trial Chamber denied the Prosecution's request for essentially two reasons which summarised the whole history. First, the evidence showed that Mr. Kabashi was still unwilling to testify and there was no reason to believe that his position was likely to change; and secondly, the Judge's comments didn't amount to a material change of circumstances because Mr. Kabashi had been under a legal obligation to testify from the very outset and had already been charged with contempt of the Tribunal so that the threat of arrest, prosecution, and imprisonment had not altered his position up until that time. Indeed he'd made it clear that he would go to prison rather than testify, and in those circumstances the Trial Chamber concluded that the prospect of contempt proceedings -- yet further contempt proceedings before a national court couldn't constitute a sufficient change of circumstances to justify re-opening the evidence at that very late stage of the proceedings. Now, Mr. President, without me reiterating the reasoning of the Trial Chamber, we respectfully submit that that decision is unassailable. And in short, as far as Mr. Kabashi is concerned, we say that in each of its decisions concerning Shefqet Kabashi the Trial Chamber paid due and proper regard to the interests of the Prosecution and the need to ensure that the proceedings were fairly conducted. The Chamber was faced with a witness who resolutely and repeatedly refused to testify and was well aware of the consequences from the outset. The Prosecution was given ample opportunity to call the witness, and the Trial Chamber rightly rejected each of the applications that was made after the 20th of November. There was not a shred of evidence that he would ever be willing to testify. And, Mr. President, that remains the position today. I'm going to come back to this at the end of my submissions, but we are in exactly the same position today as far as both of these witnesses are being concerned, that you're being asked to overturn the Trial Chamber's decision and order a re-trial when the Prosecution hasn't the slightest reason to believe that either of these witnesses would testify at any re-trial. Can I move, though, to the alternative proposition, that somehow the evidence of these witnesses ought to have been introduced by the Trial Chamber in documentary form. And let me deal first with what the Prosecution did apply for. In its 25th of October motion the Prosecution requested, as an alternative to compelled videolink, the admission into evidence of Mr. Kabashi's witness statements - and that is both of them - and his previous testimony in the Limaj case, and they made that application under, first of all, 92 quater and then in respect of the statements alone they suggested that as an alternative if they couldn't meet the requirements of 92 quater the problem could be met by calling the OTP investigator who interviewed Mr. Kabashi to testify about the contents of his witness statements. And in the course of its ruling on the 26th of November, the Trial Chamber rejected both of those applications. It held, inevitably, that the requirements of Rule 92 quater could not be met because Mr. Kabashi was neither unable to testify through death or illness nor was he untraceable. And the contents of his statements - and this is important in our submission - could not properly be adduced through an investigator since they concerned the acts and conducts of the accused and were largely uncorroborated. So the Trial Chamber conducted an evaluative balance based on the facts that his statements contained allegations against the accused directly and were largely uncorroborated and concluded on that basis that their admission would be prejudicial to the Defence because there would be no opportunity to test the veracity of the statements. Now, as far as the applications that the Prosecution did make are concerned, we say those rulings were plainly and inevitably correct. The provisions of 92 quater were clearly inapplicable, and the Trial Chamber was fully entitled to conclude, in its discretion and its appreciation of the facts, that the introduction of statements concerning the acts and conduct of the accused through the hearsay evidence of a Prosecution investigator would be unduly prejudicial. And in respect of those rulings, the Prosecution has completely failed to show - and as we understand it no longer even alleges - that the Trial Chamber erred in law in either of the rulings that it made. As far as we can understand Mr. Kremer's position, he's not suggesting that those rulings were wrong. But what he now suggests, and clearly came to this view after the appeal brief had been filed and presumably since there's been no further filing some short time before this hearing, is that Rule 89(F) provided an independent route by which to introduce the statements separately from the provisions of Rule 92 bis, ter, and quater. And that really calls - and it's a submission only developed today, as I say - but it really calls just for a moment's reflection on the relationship between Rule 89(F) and the Rule 92 series, means by which written statements can be admitted. Mr. President, we respectfully submit that insofar as it permits the admission of written statements in the interests of justice, Rule 89(F) is a general provision and Rule 92 bis, ter, and quater together represent the lex specialis for the determination of the admission of witness statements. And more particularly, the general requirement in 89(F) that the decision must be based on the interests of justice is then much more carefully calibrated in the balance between the Prosecution and the Defence which is struck by Rule 92 bis, ter, and quater. So 92 bis permits the statement to go in in lieu of oral testimony, but only where it is a statement which does not concern directly the acts and conduct of the accused. I mean, curiously here one of the suggestions Mr. Kremer makes is that even if he can't get the witnesses you should order a re-trial and the Trial Chamber should then admit the statements under Rule 89(F) but borrowing the requirements of Rule 92 bis. Well, were that the case, you would be authorising the admission of witness statements which did not concern the acts and conduct of the accused. And it's in effect a self-defeating argument for the Prosecution to come to the Appeals Chamber and to say, "You should overturn the judgement of the Trial Chamber in order to enable us to introduce statements that don't concern the acts and conduct of the accused." That is in effect what Mr. Kremer is suggesting ought to be the outcome of this appeal. But, 92 bis, 92 ter, and 92 quater together represent a calibrated means of determining what the interests of justice in Rule 89(F) require. And we respectfully submit, and if the point call for a decision we respectfully invite you to decide it in this way, that there is no room between 89(F) and 92 bis, ter, and quater for the admission of witness statements which do not meet the requirements of 92 bis, ter, and quater. One is the lex specialis for the other and looking at it another way at the very least it's a fundamental axiom of interpretation that the Rules must be construed as a whole and in a manner which makes one rule consistent with the other. And if Rule 89(F) permitted the introduction of statements which did not fall within Rule 92 bis, ter, or quater, then each of the requirements -- the qualifying steps in those sub-rules would be otiose. They'd be unnecessary. Indeed, the provisions themselves would be unnecessary if there were a wider and more general discretion to admit. But were that so even, the fact is the Prosecution here made no such application, and not only did it make no such application but they must be taken, in our submission, to have waived any argument of that nature. It would be a wholly novel approach to take an argument as we have observed conceived at the very last minute by the Prosecution on the hoof, we respectfully submit that the Trial Chamber can hardly, in those circumstances, be halted for failing to appreciate it. And moreover, the Trial Chamber must be taken to be familiar with the Rules as a whole and the way that they interact and to have exercised their decisions when they clearly were extremely anxious about the evidence of these witnesses, exercised each of their judgements against a background of a full familiarity of the way in which the Rules worked. So in the absence of a direct submission or application from the Prosecution which was rejected, we would respectfully submit that the approach of the Trial Chamber is unassailable as far as Shefqet Kabashi is concerned. And as far as the other witness is concerned the Prosecution never at any stage applied under any provision for the admission of his witness statements into evidence. I'll come to that in just a moment if I may. The other witness had told the Prosecution that he wasn't willing to testify before the trial began. On the 9th of January he told the Prosecution that he wouldn't give evidence and that his decision was final. He wasn't contacted again for nearly five months. On the 1st of May the Prosecution spoke to him and he told them that he wasn't prepared to testify, and if he was compelled to appear he wouldn't say anything at all in his evidence. He said that he wasn't interested in any form of cooperation with the OTP and that he didn't want to be contacted again. He repeated that position to a member of the Victims and Witnesses Service on the 23rd of May, although at that point he added some information about a heart condition which in the end proved irrelevant. On the 12th of June, the Trial Chamber granted the Prosecution's

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Tribunal on the 26th of June. The memorandum of service recorded again that he would not appear in court and he duly failed to appear in answer to the summons on the 26th of June. On the 7th of July, the OTP senior trial attorney and an

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: testify, either in person or via videolink, and emphatically said that he wouldn't assist the Tribunal in any way --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
