utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: He also, the other witness at this stage, declined to enter a witness protection scheme. And on the 16th of August the Prosecution applied for an order requesting that the national authorities in his country of residence compelled him to testify via videolink. Despite Defence objections, the Trial Chamber granted the motion on the 14th of September and in order to accommodate the videolink the Prosecution applied for and was granted an extension of the closure of its case so that the videolink could take place between the 13th and the 15th of November, but on the 9th of November -- and I should just point out in our -- at paragraph 76 of our appeal brief there is a date error, it should be the 9th of November not the 9th of September. On the 9th of November, VWS informed the Prosecution that the other witness wasn't going to come to the videolink because he wasn't prepared to do so. He had been visited by a police liaison officer who served the subpoena on him. The officer recorded in terms that the witness remained a staunch and defiant refusal, those were his words, to testify and was fiercely adamant that he wouldn't attend the location of the videolink. Preparations were nonetheless made for the videolink to proceed as planned, and a member of the Registry staff travelled to the other witness's country of residence for the purpose. As expected, he failed to attend on the 13th. Arrangements were then made to arrest him and transport him to the location of the videolink. He was arrested on the night of the 14th of November and taken into custody. And this requires a -- just a little detailed consideration. So he's arrested on the night of the 14th, he's taken into custody, then the following morning he appeared in a national court with the benefit of legal counsel. And in the course of that hearing he agreed to go to the location of the videolink but said, with the advice of counsel and on the record, that he would not testify if he did. So it's against that context that the hearing took place on the 15th, with a witness who had said that he would go to the hearing but he would not answer any questions that were asked of him. The problem was that there were then a number of delays in the flight schedule and due to those delays and the time differences, the situation arose whereby he couldn't appear before the Trial Chamber until after 7.00 p.m. when the hearing was due to end. I want to - against that context - come back to Judge Liu's question to Mr. Kremer about the circumstances in which this adjournment took place. In its appeal brief, and I think in his oral submissions, Mr. Kremer criticises the Trial Chamber for not making arrangements to sit beyond 7.00 p.m. or for hearing the testimony of the witness on the 16th. Now, without checking the background arrangements - and I'm doing this from recollection so I may be wrong, but I'm sure Mr. Monkhouse will remember or a member of the Registry staff will be able to check the records - there were compelling administrative reasons why the 16th was not an appropriate date to set. I believe it was to do with other judicial commitments but I can't be absolutely certain of that and that can be bottomed out if need be, but you will recall that we made the point in our appeal brief that when the Prosecution applied, as they very shortly afterwards did, for a further extension of their case, they conceded that it was impossible for the Judges to sit beyond 7.00 and that it was impossible for them to sit on the 16th. And they certainly never made any application that the Trial Chamber should continue with a witness whose evidence would have taken -- it was listed to take three days, should have started and had any meaningful attempts at hearing the witness's evidence after 7.00 in the evening. But leaving all of that aside, and indeed leaving the reasons aside, the complaint is in any event completely he devoid of substance because the Trial Chamber gave the Prosecution another opportunity to call the witness a few days later. In other words, the Prosecution made an application on the 16th, the day following the aborted videolink,

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: (redacted). The Defence objected but again the Trial Chamber overruled Defence objections and ruled in favour of the Prosecution and arrangements were made for the videolink to proceed on the 26th of November. So to -- whatever the position may have been on the evening of the 15th is rather academic, given that a further opportunity was then granted to the Prosecution a few days later. But on the 23rd of November, that is, three days before the videolink was scheduled to take place, the Prosecution informed the Trial Chamber that this witness had been hospitalised on psychiatric grounds and would not be available to testify on the 26th. And the Prosecution said that the psychiatrist was expected to re-assess his state within seven to ten days. Just pausing there for a moment. We're now three days before the date listed for the videolink to take place. The witness has been admitted to a psychiatric hospital. The indications are that his state will be re-assessed in seven to ten days, but leaving aside the psychiatric condition, we were dealing with a witness who wasn't prepared to give evidence, whether he was brought before a court or not. I'm not standing here in a position to challenge or concede whether he was genuinely psychiatrically ill. The information was that he had been admitted to a psychiatric hospital. Whether that was a device for avoiding giving evidence or a genuine illness, one simply doesn't know, but clearly the Prosecution in receipt of that information were faced with a dilemma. They had various routes available to them to seek to pursue the matter. They could have applied to the Judges for an extension of time in order to obtain the medical evidence. Did they do that? No, they did not. They could have applied to the Judges to admit his evidence under 92 quater on the grounds that he was unfit. Did they consider doing that? No, they did not. They appeared simply, in front of the Trial Chamber on Monday, the 26th, when the videolink was due to go ahead and were invited by the Trial Chamber in terms to update them as to the position. They were given every opportunity. If they really thought they were going to get this witness and that fairness required him to be called, they had every opportunity at that stage to say, "Well we've been told he's in hospital but we have good reason to believe he will be re-assessed in seven to ten days and he may even change his mind at that stage," and to make an application to the judges to adjourn for seven to ten days to await the outcome of the medical analysis. But the only submission that the senior OTP Prosecutor made on that day was to repeat the information that he had been hospitalised and was liable to be re-assessed. They made no applications whatsoever. Significantly, they didn't seek an adjournment either to secure his evidence or to secure medical evidence. Despite having been aware for three days of the position and having ample opportunity to do it, they didn't seek the admission of his witness statements in any form, never mind 89(F), they didn't seek to do it through 92 quater. I mean, with the greatest of respect to Mr. Kremer and avoiding all possibility of hindsight, it's difficult to resist the conclusion that the Prosecution had given up on the witness. They had come to the conclusion by the end of the case that this was not a witness who was ever going to testify. And it's certainly clear that the Prosecution made a considered decision not to apply for more time and clear also that they never applied to the Trial Chamber for an opportunity to re-open their case, and even as we stand here today you are not being told that this is a witness who is either fit or is willing to give evidence. Now -- so they now complain insufficient time was given by the Trial Chamber, but we say that is a surprising submission in view of the fact that the Prosecution simply made no such applications. If, as we say, they considered either that the requirements of a fair trial required more time or that the requirements of a fair trial required the admission of a witness statement, the material -- the Rules were there to enable them to make the application. They wouldn't even have needed to come up with the novel and inventive approach of trying to create a separate free-standing basis under 89(F) because they had Rule 92 quater available to them had they chosen to use it. But they must, no doubt, had come to the conclusion that it would not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I just take you back to the question of the relationship as you see it --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- between 89(F) and 92 bis, ter, and quater rules. You're saying that 89(F) does not provide any basis for admission that is independent of 92 bis, ter, and quater?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, we make a two-fold submission. The first submission is that 92 bis, ter, and quater are lex specialis to deal with the interest of justice test in 89(F). And, indeed, if that were not so they would have no purpose at all because 89(F) would permit the Trial Chamber to admit statements whenever they considered it to be in the interests of justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember the Appeals Chamber -- this Chamber has said something on that relationship. I'll be reminded of it shortly by one of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. But even if we're wrong in putting the submission quite as starkly as we do -- and I have to say in our submission it is clear that that is the right construction of the Rules because there would be no point in having 92 ter, bis, and quater if 89(F) provided a free-standing method for admission. They -- but even if we're wrong about that, 89(F) specifically is qualified by an interest of justice calibration. And Rule 92 bis, ter, and quater tell you when it will be in the interests of justice. So, for example, if the witness isn't available to be cross-examined and it's going in under 92 bis it cannot concern the acts and conduct of the accused because the interests of justice would then militate against its admission. If, on the other hand, it's a 92 quater case and the reasons for the witness's absence are illness or death or untraceability, then the fact that it concerns the acts and conduct of the accused is not an absolute bar but is a strong reason against the admission of the statement according to the rule itself. In other words, there is a calibrated interests of justice test within 92 bis, ter, and quater. So the first submission that we make is that that is the lex specialis and 89(F) leaves no room for the admission of statements outside of those provisions, and if there is to be a mechanism of the sort that is proposed by the Prosecution here with some alternative mechanism for perhaps intimidated witnesses were that to be found --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kremer, in your reply you'll want to address this.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- it would need, in our submission, to be dealt with by -- achieved by means of an amendment to the Rules. But, Mr. President, in answer to your question, if we're wrong in putting the matter as starkly as that, one thing is certain is that it's an axiom of construction that the Rules must be read as a whole. In other words, it cannot be the case that one could admit through 89(F) a statement that -- the admission of which would conflict with Rule 92. So if, for example, you had the witness statement of a witness whose evidence concerned the acts and conduct of the accused but it could not be brought within Rule 92 quater and the witness was not available for cross-examination so that neither 92 ter nor 92 quater could apply, it could not be the case, in our submission, that such a statement could be admitted under Rule 89(F) if it concerned the acts and conduct of the accused when to do so would directly conflict with the injunction in Rule 92 bis. That's the way that we put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And it is conceded that these statements go to the acts and conduct --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It is conceded. Indeed, the reason -- that's why I said it was significant. The reason why the Trial Chamber wouldn't let the Prosecution admit Shefqet Kabashi's statement through it being read by an investigator was because the Trial Chamber took the view that it concerned the acts and conduct of the accused, was largely uncorroborated, and that it would be unfair to the Defence, therefore, to admit it. So it conducted that balancing exercise, albeit within the context of an application to have the statement read by an investigator, but if they're right -- and the Prosecution don't appeal that balancing exercise, they're not suggesting that was wrong; but if they're not suggesting that was wrong, it couldn't be admitted under 89(F) in the interests of justice either because as precisely the same balance would be required. And if the Prosecution concede that Trial Chamber got the balance right when considering whether a Prosecution investigator should be called to give evidence of the contents of the statement; namely, that it would be unfair to the accused because it concerned acts and conduct, was uncorroborated, and couldn't be cross-examined, those factors equally would prevent its admission under 89(F) in our submission. How could it be in the interests of justice to admit it and yet not in the interest of justice to have it read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have just about five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I've very nearly finished. Mr. President, can I just tie-up the loose ends on (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We say, putting it shortly, the Trial Chamber can't be faulted on appeal for failing to make orders that the Prosecution didn't ask them to make at trial. The result of the history with that -- the other witness is this: The Trial Chamber never made an adverse ruling to the Prosecution. They never ever made a ruling against the Prosecution in relation to the admission of the other witness's testimony. Every application the Prosecution made to secure the other witness's evidence was granted, but the witness himself steadfastly refused to give evidence, twice failed to respond to a subpoena, and had then had himself admitted to hospital just as he was about to be called a third time. There is, we say simply, no basis now for the Prosecution to argue now that there should have been a further adjournment, in the absence of an application for one, for what must have been an unspecified and indefinite period of time, at that very late stage of the trial, on the basis of a speculative hope that this witness might recover from his psychiatric if condition if he really had one and then change his mind and agree testify despite his previous consistent refusals to do it. Mr. President, it's well settled in the Tribunal's case law that an appeal against discretionary rulings of this kind is limited to establishing whether the Trial Chamber abused its discretion by committing a discernible error. We say that the decisions of the Trial Chamber in relation to these two witnesses don't begin to meet that threshold. In our submission, the approach of the Trial Chamber wasn't merely reasonable but was plainly right and it can't sensibly be suggested that there's any abuse of discretion here. Whether viewed individually or collectively, the Trial Chamber's approach to the testimony of these witnesses was appropriate and, we say, inevitable and that, as I foreshadowed a little earlier in my submissions, is underlined by the position that we find ourselves in today. Even now the Prosecution are not able to tell you that either witness would give evidence if the case were brought on a re-trial. So the overwhelming likelihood from the history thus far were a re-trial to be ordered is that they would maintain their refusal to testify. And were that the case, Mr. Kremer's fall-back position is that their statements might be admitted under 89(F) and 92 bis read together. In other words, as I said to your -- to the Chamber a little earlier, the Prosecution is suggesting -- seriously seeking to suggest that the verdict of the Trial Chamber should be overturned with -- on the theoretical prospect that statements that do not concern the acts and conduct of the accused could then be adduced at what would be, in effect, a pointless re-trial. Those are our submissions. Is there any particular matter I could help you with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not really, Mr. Emmerson. We're grateful to you for your submissions. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have but a moment and Ms. Rohan will be presenting our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROHAN
utterances.text: Actually, good afternoon, Your Honours, and thank you for this opportunity to talk to you briefly about ground three, which is the ground that I'm going to address. We -- before I do, the Defence for Mr. Balaj joins in the arguments which were just presented by Mr. Emmerson regarding ground one. And in light of the fact that the Prosecution has presented no arguments regarding ground two, we will submit that on the briefs that we have filed. We stand by the arguments presented in those briefs and believe that the acquittal was properly returned as to the count in question. As for ground three, before I get into the substance of it I want to make just a very short comment on the standard of appellate review for factual errors. I of course know that this Chamber knows what that standard is and I make the comments only to put in perspective the remainder of my argument. It's clear under the case law of this Tribunal that when an error of fact is asserted on appeal, there is of course no de novo review. The decision of the Trial Court is entitled to deference. Factual findings are not lightly disturbed on appeal. The appellate chamber, as wise as it may be, does not substitute its judgement regarding the facts for the judgement of the Trial Chamber. And there is also a recognition that reasonable minds may differ and, therefore, reasonable Judges may differ. That does not make a factual finding inappropriate. So what is the test for reasonableness and in order to find a factual error on appeal there must be a finding that that finding of fact was unreasonable and the test is this: It's whether the evidence relied on by the Trial Chamber could not have been accepted by any reasonable trier of fact. Could not have been accepted by any reasonable trier of fact or where the evaluation of the evidence is wholly erroneous. And this test exists in conjunction with the presumption that the Trial Chamber has considered all of the evidence unless there's an affirmative showing that it has not, that it considered all of the evidence that was presented to it. And in this case, I would say the Trial Chamber certainly as all counts clearly defined the legal principles, gave an exhaustive analysis of the facts as presented by the witnesses, a rendition of the testimony, and an analysis of those facts and the law as applied to those facts. Clearly, there was a thorough review of the evidence which was presented. So now on appeal what is the Prosecution's burden given this situation? And the burden is that if they can show a factual error - and I submit they cannot - if they can show an error of fact then they must also show in addition to that that when account is taken for that error all reasonable doubt has been eliminated. And I submit that there -- simply -- the standard simply has not been met in this case regarding ground three which relates, as we know, to the rape of Witness 61, cruel treatment of Witness 1. Now, the background to that count, there was a discussion this morning about the facts of the rape. The fact that the victim was raped was not disputed at trial. That's not in dispute here either. The fundamental issue, the only issue, was the identity of the assailant. And I found it odd that the Prosecution in its brief suggested that the Trial Court was unreasonable on focusing on that and saying does the evidence show that Witness 61 was raped by Mr. Balaj or another KLA soldier. That was the issue in dispute at trial. Clearly it was reasonable for the Trial Chamber to focus on that issue, and this morning a comment was made that the Trial Chamber gave undue emphasis regarding Witness 61's inability to identify Mr. Balaj. I'm going to return to that factually in a moment. That was the only issue, so it is not surprising that the Trial Court gave some emphasis to credible, reliable, evidence presented by Witness 61 regarding her inability to identify Mr. Balaj. And I submit that that evidence on its own raised a reasonable doubt under any standard that is used at this Tribunal. Certainly, there's no showing that in finding a reasonable doubt the Trial Court ignored any evidence. And what was the evidence relied on by the Trial Court? The very first and probably the most important is that Witness 61 stated when she was brought up to headquarters and brought into a room where these events occurred, that the light was on, that she was seated across the table from the man who raped her, and that she was questioned for 30 minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you for a minute. I'm very sorry to do so. Mr. Emmerson, when you asked if there was anything else I wanted to hear you on there was. I was thinking about it. I would like to hear you later on - and the Prosecution as well - on the question of the relationship between the two sets of rules in light of the Slobodan Milosevic decision and also the Galic decision. I'm sorry, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROHAN
utterances.text: Perfectly okay. What was the evidence? The evidence was that Witness 61 was in the room with a man who raped her for 30 minutes, a lighted room, seated at a table, being questioned. And in fact when this evidence was adduced at trial the Trial Chamber at one point interrupted the questioning about it and said essentially: We understand what you're saying. It's not within the Trial Chamber's thinking process at this point that she did not have a clear opportunity to see this man; she did. And that's at transcript number 4039. In addition to that 30 minutes in a lit room, then there was one and a half hours in a room that was semi-lit. The light was turned off, but the witness testified that there was a television on, and she still saw the face of the assailant for another hour and a half. And we've all been in rooms where televisions were on, you have a sense of what that lighting may be like. It's a semi-lit room. It does provide some opportunity for observation. Then after that she testified that after she went home she saw the man who raped her again in the village, her village. She saw him driving by. And in her evidence in chief she said this happened one time. She later confirmed, however, that she had told the Office of the Prosecution in a statement before trial that this had happened often, she had seen him often in the village after this happened, which suggests that she was fully capable of recognising this man. Nevertheless, she never identified Mr. Balaj as being this man and she was given plenty of opportunity. She was shown a photo-board in 2002 - true, it was some time after the event - although the witness testified very clearly, and it's understandable, that this was an unforgettable event for her. She would never forget it. In 2002 shown a picture of Mr. Balaj in a photo-board, she did not recognise anyone as the assailant. In 2005 she and her family were watching television, Mr. Balaj appears on television with a news story that he is charged with a crime. His name is there, Idriz Balaj, now associated with the name Toger, and her family says - according to her testimony on oath - that's Toger, see that's Toger. And what does she say? The man didn't look like Toger to me, he looked older, he looked older. And I have to say, and this morning there was a comment made of perhaps the reason that he looked older was that time passed, but when she testified she testified that the man who actually raped her was about 20 or 21 years old. Mr. Balaj, being 26 or 27 at the time. And described him as young. Now she sees Mr. Balaj on television and says again he looks -- he looks older than the man who raped me, and I am wondering why we refuse to believe this woman. She is the only person who saw the man who raped her, and she is saying it's not Mr. Balaj. Somehow we are not to accept that evidence and not believe her. I don't think that's logical. I don't think it's the way the law meant to operate. Certainly, it was cause to find a reasonable doubt as to whether Mr. Balaj had been properly identified. Finally she did describe the man who assailed her as someone with black hair who spoke Albanian, which was true of probably 90 per cent of the people in the area at the time. But what was important was the difference in height, and again this morning we heard that height was not material, height was not material. Well, I would submit that it was material, however that's really not the inquiry here. The inquiry was is it unreasonable for the Trial Court to have considered that the difference in height may be something that indicates that there's a reasonable doubt that Mr. Balaj committed this crime, and I think it was perfectly reasonable. Certainly, this is the kind of evidence that would be accepted by a reasonable trier of fact. It was not an insignificant difference. The witness is actually a very small, short woman. She said that the individual who assailed her was only a little taller than her, a small man, and the record reflects that there were measurements taken of Mr. Balaj. He is not a short man and he is bigger than the individual described by the victim here. So in sum, the evidence before the Trial Chamber that had to be considered in my opinion -- not in my opinion, it was actually all undisputed evidence. There was no dispute. The Defence didn't put on any affirmative evidence in this case. No dispute as to this. What was the evidence? Mr. Balaj doesn't fit the physical description of the assailant. The victim had a very clear view of the man who assailed her, the Prosecution agrees to this in their brief, that the victim had a clear view. Of all the witnesses or the information on this count that was adduced on in the Trial Court, the only person who actually saw the individual was the victim, Victim [sic] 61, she's the one who saw the person. It's not surprising. Therefore, the Trial Court didn't rely on hearsay on cross-examined statements from Witness 1 who was not present when this happened. She did not identify Mr. Balaj. Affirmatively said he did not look like Toger for whatever reason. It doesn't matter what the reason is. She said he didn't look like Toger. Mr. Balaj didn't look like the man she thought was Toger, and there were others present at the scene who could have been the perpetrator. There's no dispute about that either. The law requires that in a circumstantial evidence reasoning process, it's not sufficient that a reasonable inference can be drawn when arriving at a finding of guilt. When arriving at a finding of guilt it has to be the only reasonable inference that can be drawn, and I submit that the Trial Court, given those standards, properly found reasonable doubt that the undisputed evidence had established that Mr. Balaj was the perpetrator of this crime. In addition, there is this theory now that's been offered by the Prosecution here on appeal about how the assailant somehow had to be Toger and -- or Mr. Balaj, and I think that in some senses that relies on -- well, two things. One, this is not a de novo review, and really in positing this theory the Prosecution is asking the Court to re-interpret the evidence. They haven't, in my submission, pointed out a factual error, an unreasonable finding. They really are arguing there's another way to look at the evidence and chances are there are and there may be several ways of looking at the evidence, but that's not their burden here and that's not the standard here. In addition, they rely on some aspects of the record that I submit are incorrect, and I -- of course things are subject to interpretation, but a very large one that the victim -- Witness 61 saw Toger inside her house. And I would -- before the individuals were moved up to the headquarters. And I would submit that the record simply doesn't support that at all. Her testimony at transcript 3982 was that they came inside. The testimony was quite ambiguous, they came inside. Thereafter she testified at page 4043 that she heard the name of Toger for the first time when she was outside of the house. So there's a real ambiguity as to what she saw or did not see inside the house. However, the ambiguity, of course, could have been clarified immediately at trial when Witness 61 was seated in the courtroom. The simple question: Was the assailant, the man who actually raped you, one of the men you saw inside your house that night? That question was never asked. So the record remains ambiguous on that point. Therefore, the record does not prove that point beyond a reasonable doubt. The Trial Chamber had ample cause to find reasonable doubt. I think I have -- regarding the final count of ground three, and that has to do with Witness 1, the cruel treatment of Witness 1, the Prosecution has alleged this as a legal error. In my submission, this is really a factual error masquerading as a legal one to get a better standard of review on appeal perhaps or for whatever reason. The Trial Court clearly knew what the law was, what constituted cruel treatment. It's quoted in its opinion. It found on the facts that the fact that Witness 1 was put into a well just didn't constitute cruel treatment under the jurisprudence at the Tribunal. And we've all seen examples of cruel treatment, use of people as human shields in Blaskic or forced labour, prison camp conditions, shelling of a civilian town, these are examples of cruel treatment. And while being placed in a well may not be a very pleasant experience, whether it rises to the dignity - if I can use that term - of cruel treatment was certainly a question that the Trial Court, in my submission, resolved properly, which is that it did not. There's also been an argument presented that there was severe mental distress caused to Witness 1 because of this. Now, the difficulty with that argument is that it's based on speculation, complete speculation. There's no statement from Witness 1 as to what his mental state was. He could have been asked at the time he was interviewed pre-trial. He obviously was not available at trial as we know. He did not describe the mental state that the Prosecution attributes to him now. But finally, and perhaps most importantly, Mr. Balaj - separate from the JCE on which he was acquitted - the theory of liability for him on this count was that he committed it, this count, or that he planned it. And whether putting someone in a well constitutes cruel treatment or not, there was simply no evidence that Mr. Balaj committed this crime. In fact, Witness 1 says it was two other people. And certainly no evidence of planning. The record is silent on that point. So I would submit, unless Your Honours have any questions, that the Trial Court's finding of reasonable doubt as to Count 36, rape, was not based on any unreasonable factual findings, that it must be sustained, that the acquittal must be sustained, and that the same is true as to the cruel treatment of Witness 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm grateful to you, Ms. Rohan, for your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Counsel, given the context of Kosovo at the time of the events in question, isn't it almost certain that Witness 1 would have worried about his wife's welfare as he stood trapped inside the well while she was taken to the KLA house? Doesn't this constitute serious mental suffering?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROHAN
utterances.text: I have no doubt that he was worried. The problem I have with that submission is that there is no evidence there. The witness was available to be questioned about this prior to trial and to provide evidence on this. He said nothing along the lines of what the Prosecution has proposed here. So would we, us, in that situation feel that we; yes, I think many people would. But it's difficult to know or to extrapolate as to what Witness 1 would feel. So my first submission is that there is no evidence of that. We could speculate, yes. There could be even a reasonable probability, yes. But the proof of the crime requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt. That I think is lacking here, in addition to the fact that the modes of liability were not proved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break now for one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: It may well assist Your Honours to know that as far as the case of Lahi Brahimaj is concerned, on this matter in terms of responding to the Prosecution's appeal, we respectfully adopt everything that has been so ably said by Mr. Emmerson, and we understand that, of course, the Chamber's concern about the inter-relationship between 92 bis and 89(F), as you've already expressed in relation to both the Galic and Milosevic decisions, both Milosevic at first instance and on appeal. We know that Mr. Emmerson is well seized of these matters, and we can happily rely on him to address Your Honours further on that. We will have nothing further to add. So that will at least shorten Your Honours' day by 55 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are grateful for that and I am happy to see the confidence that you repose in Mr. Emmerson and certainly it's well placed. We will adjourn for -- no. Mr. Emmerson, you have the two cases?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, may I borrow a little of what would have been Mr. Harvey's time just to deal with it. It won't take very long .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We'll work something out. Thank you. We'll adjourn. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.32 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- before you begin, Mr. Kremer, the Chamber has been considering the two statements which are in the annex. Now, it may be that you might want the Chamber to give consideration to those two statements; and if that is so, then you might consider making an application under Rule 115 for the admission of those statements as additional evidence. Of course, the requirements have to be met and we would briefly hear from the other parties. But this is entirely a matter for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm sorry. If the Chamber is asking for the submission to be made orally, I can do so at the close of the proceedings. If you would prefer that it be made in writing, I'm certainly prepared to do that on a very short term. If -- it was my consideration when filing the notice of appeal that the context of the statements help define the relevance of this testimony in the context of the witness intimidation. If it's necessary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- to get it in as evidence before us is through the route of 115.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Then I would move to have it -- have the statements admitted under Rule 115 and ask the Court's leave to file a written motion within seven days to be responded to by the Defence in whatever time the Court deems appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we would prefer if you -- if the application were made orally and we would hear from the other side as well. I don't think this is a matter that has to be done in the way that you have suggested. Mr. Emmerson would have a chance to reply later. But I'm not asking you to do it right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Oh, I thought you were asking me to do it right now. I'm just buying for a little time, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not immediately, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Perhaps at the end of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I reserve our position in respect both of the substance of such an application --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- and indeed of the procedure by which it would then have been made because obviously it requires consideration of questions, whether the evidence should have been regarded as having been available at the time of trial, whether it's credible - which obviously we're not in a position to argue because the Prosecution hasn't made the application timeously. And that would be a prerequisite for it's submission before the Trial Chamber could consider it. And, indeed, the rule appears to contemplate only the possibility of an application being made before or at the hearing and not subsequent to it. And so if one looks at the provisions of Rule 115(C), the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us attend to that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And I think one would also need, with respect, to ask with for what purpose would the statement be being adduced. The rule is primarily aimed for the introduction of fresh evidence to consider matters on the merits, and the Prosecution have never suggested and can't, in effect, suggest that the statements could form now part of the record upon which consideration of the appeal would proceed because, of course, the Defence never had an opportunity at trial to answer them, they not having been adduced by the Prosecution in the course of its case. So I think there may be some other complex questions about whether it's proper for the Prosecution, not having made the application in advance, to make an application in that rather difficult and complex and novel nature in the course of the hearing. In effect, it doesn't alter the substance of the arguments which are arguments about whether the Trial Chamber acted appropriately or not. Can I then turn to what may in fact be dispositive, because we would respectfully submit that the decisions in Galic and then Milosevic make it abundantly clear that the first limb submission that I made is correct, namely, that these two sets of rules are -- have the relationship of lex generalis to lex specialis and that if a statement, the admission of a statement in lieu of testimony as opposed to a statement where the witness attests -- attends and attests to the truth of the statement, where the admission of a statement in lieu of oral testimony and without oral testimony from the witness is sought to be admitted, it may only be admitted pursuant to the requirements of 92 bis or now also 92 quater. 89(F) provides no residual means by which a statement can be admitted in lieu, and we respectfully submit that is entirely clear from a reading of these decision in the context of the rules as they stood at the time and have subsequently been amended. In other words, if a statement is capable of falling within 92 bis or 92 quater because it is a statement that is sought by the Prosecution to be admitted in lieu of oral testimony without the witness attending, attesting to it, and being available for cross-examination, then it must meet the requirements of one or other of those provisions in order to fall within 89(F) at all. Can I say, briefly, why it is we say that. It might be helpful if I simply set out very briefly the position in relation to the positions and how it is, in our submission, abundantly clear when one traces the thread through that that must be the case. The first, of course, is Galic 7th of June, 2002, and at that stage the state of Rule 92 was that the only provision which could authorise the admission of a written statement in lieu of testimony was 92 bis. There was no 92 ter and there was no 92 quater. And on the facts there was the issue related to one witness of fact and one expert witness, both of whom had died. There was a dispute about whether their statements concerned the acts and conduct of the accused, but it's clear that they would now fall squarely within the requirements of 92 quater, being witnesses who had died. And the issue for the Trial Chamber would be did they concern the acts and conducts of the accused; and if so, was it fair for the Defence to admit them and those parts concerned acts and conduct. The Trial Chamber admitted the statements under 92 bis. The Defence appealed contending that the Trial Chamber was wrong in its finding that they did not concern the acts and conduct of the accused. So it was a Defence appeal on the issue of whether they were concerned with acts and conduct. But the Prosecution's response was even if they were concerned with acts and conduct and therefore 92 bis was wrongly applied, the statements in any event could have gone in under 89(C) as relevant evidence. And so it was in dealing with the Prosecution's alternative submission advanced on appeal that the admission of the statements could be upheld even if 92 bis didn't apply that the relevant provisions of the judgement arise. Can I -- because we don't have them on the screen, can I just read the two short passages that appear to be of particular relevance. In paragraph 28 the Appeals Chamber is discussing Kordic and observes that: "Prior to the addition of Rule 92 bis, the statement of a witness made to an OTP investigator who had died since making it had been admitted into evidence by a Trial Chamber under 89(C)," under Rule 89(C) in Kordic. In other words, this was in a yet previous incarnation of Rule 92 where there was no equivalent of 92 bis and a general provision of 89(C) had been invoked at trial level, and the quotation goes on: "The Appeals Chamber overruled that decision on the basis that the discretion to admit hearsay evidence under Rule 89(C) had to be exercised so that it was in harmony with the Statute and the other Rules to the greatest extent possible and only where the Trial Chamber was satisfied that the evidence was reliable." Paragraph 28, the last sentence, the Appeals Chamber noted that: "Rule 92 bis as a whole is concerned with hearsay evidence, such as would previously have been admissible under Rule 89(C), but it is hearsay material of a very special type with very serious issues raised as to its reliability." And then the key passage is paragraph 31, the holding of the Appeals Chamber: "A party cannot be permitted to tender a written statement given by a perspective witness to an investigator of the OTP under Rule 89(C) in order to avoid the stringency of Rule 92 bis." So it's not possible to go under the general if the specific is capable of applying because the specific has additional safe-guards. The judgement goes on: "The purpose of Rule 92 bis is to restrict the admissibility of this very special type of hearsay to that which falls within its terms." So in other words, it is not only permitted but equally he restrictive. It excludes that which is capable of falling within it but doesn't meet its requirements. "By analogy 92 bis is the lex specialis," says the judgement, "which takes the admissibility of witness statements of perspective witnesses and transcripts of evidence out of the scope of the lex generalis of Rule 89(C); although, the general propositions which were implicit in Rule 89(C), that the evidence is admissible only if relevant, remain applicable 38." And the final sentence of that paragraph reads -- this is dealing with the Prosecution's argument that a general provision could have solved the problem on the facts. "The Prosecution argument that the two statements admitted into evidence were in any event admissible under Rule 89(C) without the restrictions of Rule 92 bis is rejected." In other words, on the Rules as they stood at the time, it wasn't possible to rely on the general provisions of Rule 89 in circumstances where 92 bis was the lex specialis. And it was therefore necessary to decide whether these were statements which concerned the acts and conduct of the accused. So that's the starting position against which one looks at the decision in Milosevic. Now, Milosevic on appeal is simply concerned with what we would now routinely treat as 92 quater procedure. The witness is there but -- and is available for cross-examination, but in order to save time the witness is invited to read through their witness statement and confirm the contents of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I do apologise, that was a slip of the tongue. Yes, I'm sorry. Under Rule 92 ter, so the witness will attest to the correctness of the witness statement, adopt it as his oral testimony, and then answer questions on it in cross-examination. And of course at the time of the Milosevic first instance and appeal decisions, Rule 92 ter did not exist. And so the question was: Could the general provisions of Rule 89(F) permit the adducing of the written statement to stand as evidence in chief providing it was attested to and the witness was available for cross-examination? And the Appeals Chamber held that the answer was yes and that a procedure, which is now replicated in Rule 92 ter, was capable of being read into the proceedings under Rule 89(F). But the reason for that was because this was not, said the Appeals Chamber, as in Galic, a situation where the provisions of Rule 92 bis applied. If it was a case where 92 bis applied because what was being sought was the admission of a statement in lieu of evidence, that is to say not oral testimony adopting it but a statement in lieu, then it had to be brought within 92 bis, that being the only exception at the time. The reason the lex specialis didn't apply to what is now regarded as 92 ter proceedings is because the witness was there and was available, so it wasn't 92 bis territory at all. And if it didn't fall within 92 bis, the lex specialis principle excluding it from 89(F) could not apply. And therefore it follows -- and if it does fall within 92 bis because it's a statement in lieu, then the exclusionary principle does apply as in Galic. And one gets that from the Milosevic decision, and it is with respect and in our submission absolutely and abundantly put beyond any doubt that the submission that the Prosecution has sought to suggest should have been self-evident to the Trial Chamber was not only not self-evident it was abundantly unarguable had the Prosecution chosen to raise it because it would not have been permitted within the rules. At paragraph 16 of the judgement: "The Appeals Chamber is satisfied that -- the Appeals Chamber is satisfied that the fact that the witness is present and can orally attest to the accuracy of the written statement is sufficient to place this application beyond the scope of Rule 92 bis. Where the witness is present before the Court and orally attests to the accuracy of the statement, the evidence entered into the record cannot be considered to be exclusively written evidence within the meaning of Rule 92 bis. The testimony of the witness constitutes a mixture of oral and written evidence. The appearance of the witness in court to attest to a written statement is a crucial factor which rendered 92 bis inapplicable. The fact that a witness may merely give a brief oral statement to the effect that the written statement is accurate does not alter this conclusion." In other words, the decisive fact that rendered 92 bis inapplicable was the very fact that the witness was attending to give oral evidence about the correctness of the statement and be available for cross-examination. And since 92 bis was inapplicable the lex specialis rule that excluded a more general approach to 89(F) did not apply. The Appeals Chamber went on at paragraph 17 on the same issue: "Additionally," it said, "the determination of this evidence," that is the statements admitted in a 92 ter form, that "this evidence constitutes written evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis despite the appearance of the witness would be an unduly formalistic interpretation. Were the witness, for example, allowed by the court to read verbatim from the statement, the evidence in question would be considered oral evidence and, therefore, not subject to the restrictions imposed by Rule 92 bis. "In effect," this is paragraph 18, "in effect, the fact that a written statement has been prepared for the purposes of legal proceedings does not, by itself, suffice to make it admissible only under Rule 92 bis unless the statement is also intended to be in lieu of oral evidence." Can I just read that paragraph again because it's absolutely the fulcrum. "In effect, the fact that a written statement has been prepared for the purposes of legal proceedings," that is, of course, these statements, "does not, by itself, suffice to make it admissible only under Rule 92 bis unless the statement is also intended to be in lieu of oral evidence." So putting it another way, if the statement is intended to be in lieu of oral evidence, it may only be admitted under Rule 92 bis as the Rules then stood. And applying that interpretation here, there's simply no possibility at all, without an amendment to the Rules, of having some general provision that would allow the introduction of statements not meeting the requirements of Rule 92 bis or 92 quater. And if I could finish with Milosevic at paragraph 20 just about -- below halfway down the paragraph, there are various policy considerations outlined as to why it's a good idea to move to a 92 ter-type procedure and so forth, and the Appeals Chamber observes: "Whilst these factors constitute important policy considerations, they do not go to the question of whether the evidence constitutes written evidence within the meaning of Rule 92 bis, and therefore to whether the scope of Rule 92 bis extends to this application. Nevertheless, these factors may be relevant when determining whether admitting such statements is in the interests of justice under Rule 89(F)." Now, in our submission reading the statement as a whole what is -- what becomes absolutely clear is that on the Rules as they then stood, if a statement was being admitted which fell within the rubric of 92 bis, then it could only be admitted under 92 bis because there was no residual discretion under 89(F). And that, of course, would mean that it must satisfy the acts and conducts exclusion. It couldn't be a statement which related to the acts and conduct of the accused. And that, indeed, was the very issue in Galic and the reason why the jurisprudence must be regarded as settled that the relationship is that of the general to the particular or a lex specialis relationship. Now, obviously in the light of Milosevic, 92 ter was introduced and subsequently to Galic and, indeed, at the same time I think as 92 ter 92 quater was introduced. And so in our submission the process is a very simple one. Question one that the Trial Chamber has to ask itself: Is this a situation where a statement is being admitted in lieu of oral testimony or is this a situation where a witness is intending to adopt their statement and make themselves available for cross-examination. That's the first question. If the answer is it's a case where the statement is to be admitted in lieu, then it must be brought within either 92 bis or 92 quater. Here the Prosecution applied under 92 quater in respect of Shefqet Kabashi but made no application at all in relation to the other witness. But be that as it may, what is abundantly clear is that they could never have brought these statements under 92 bis and never made the application because they concerned the acts and conduct of the accused. And if one needs to find evidence of what the approach of the Trial Chamber would have been if they had applied under 92 bis, one needn't look no further than the approach that they took to the second alternative application, to admit the statement of Shefqet Kabashi by calling the investigator who took the statements to read out their contents. And if I could just -- it's a very, very short passage from the transcript at 10978, line 25, through to 10979, line 9. In dealing with that application the Trial Chamber said this: "The second alternative put forward is that the Prosecution be allowed to re-call Prosecution investigator Barney Kelly who was present when Mr. Kabashi gave his statements so as to give hearsay evidence as to the statements provided by Mr. Kabashi to the Prosecution. The Chamber finds this way of introducing evidence which goes to the acts and conduct of the accused, much of it uncorroborated by other evidence, both inappropriate and prejudicial to the Defence, who has -- had no opportunity to test the veracity of the statements and for these reasons the Chamber denies the Prosecution's motion in its entirety. In other words, the Trial Chamber made the very finding that this was evidence that concerned acts and conduct, that it was uncorroborated in substance, and that it would be prejudicial and unfair to admit it. So even if the Prosecution were right - and we say is there's simply no room in the rules for the application that the Prosecution now says it ought to have met --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That application was made under 92 --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That application was -- there were two applications made. One was made under 92 quater, that was to read the statements and the previous testimony in Limaj. And that was rejected because the witness was neither sick, dead, nor unavailable; and an alternative application was simply made to read the statements as hearsay evidence. I don't recall, without looking at the motion, whether it was specifically made under 89(F), but it certainly -- it certainly was an application, I think it was simply put as a hearsay -- an application to call the investigator to give hearsay evidence. But the guts of the decision that the Trial Chamber to make was whether it was in the interests of justice to let the Prosecution do this, which is precisely the decision that they would have to make if they approached it under Rule 89(F). But as we respectfully submit, they could never have approached it under Rule 89(F) because this was a statement in lieu of evidence and it had to be brought within 92 bis or 92 quater. And so even if we're wrong on that principal submission, the bold fact is the Prosecution never made any such application under 89(F), never sought to suggest there was, for example, a general discretion where there was evidence of witness intimidation to adduce the statement without meeting the requirements of 92 bis or 92 quater. There was, in fact, no evidence at all of witness intimidation in relation to Shefqet Kabashi. On the contrary, the evidence from his own mouth was that no one had threatened him. As far as the other witness's concern, there was no finding made that he was intimidated. There were allegations made, but this was a witness who - for reasons I don't need to go into - his credibility was very, very substantially in doubt and whose evidence was flatly in contradiction to two witnesses that were called by the Prosecution on the central issues in the case. He was a very, very questionable issue, and there's no -- absolutely no finding by the Trial Chamber that his claims of intimidation were well founded. Nor, with respect, is there any suggestion that any one of the defendants or the accused was in any way responsible for any act of intimidation against anybody. In each of its provisional release decisions during the trial, the Trial Chamber was at great pains to emphasise that there was nothing to suggest that any act of intimidation had been done by or at the behest of any one of the accused in this case. So much what's been said to you creates a very misleading picture, but the fact is that even if there were such a general exception under 89(F), which there isn't, the application wasn't made and had it been made determinations of fact would have to have been which couldn't have been made and weren't made. But, if can I simply conclude by saying this: Even if all of those weren't complete answers to the Prosecution's appeal, it is as, we submit, clear from the ruling that I've just summarised that the Trial Chamber's view is that these statements could not properly go in without cross-examination. It simply wasn't fair. That's what they held, and we would respectfully submit that that is also a complete answer, but perhaps the most important point is the Prosecution don't challenge that finding. There's no appeal against the Trial Chamber's decision refusing to allow the Prosecutor and the investigator to read the contents of the statement on the grounds that it was prejudicial to the Defence because it concerned acts and conduct and was uncorroborated. The Prosecution aren't appealing that decision, they're not suggesting it was wrong. Indeed, Mr. Kremer said applying the Rules properly they went through all the stages and rejected all the applications that the Prosecution made, but they should somehow have thought of a new routine through 89(F). So it's conceded by the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You said earlier that the Trial Chamber clearly made the determination that the statements could not go in without cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. In connection with Shefqet Kabashi when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So on what basis would the Trial Chamber have made that determination?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It was just the passage that I just read to the Trial Chamber. On the basis that, first of all, Kabashi's statements concerned the acts and conduct of the accused; secondly, that they were uncorroborated by other evidence to a large extent; and thirdly, that in the absence of an ability to cross-examine him, it would for those reasons be unfairly prejudicial to the Defence to admit them through the calling of a Prosecution investigator. Now, that's a ruling that the Trial Chamber made and that the Prosecution does not challenge. Yes, I'm sorry -- we found -- Your Honour asked me the question under what provision was that made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We found the motion, it was made under Rule 89, just generally without specifying which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But what it comes to is this: That if there were to be some new principle of Tribunal evidential jurisprudence that was to allow a witness statement to go in in lieu of, in the absence of the witness, on the grounds that there was evidence that the witness had been intimidated, we say first of all that could only have been done by an amendment to the Rules; secondly, it would require very careful consideration of what the content of the amendment should be, it would need very careful consideration of the relevance of whether the acts and conducts of the accused should be a complete exclusion, a fact attending against or, perhaps, in some exceptional circumstances, a fact attending in favour, but it's clearly under the jurisprudence of the Appeals Chamber not something that it's open to a Trial Chamber to invent for itself. So the rubric of a lex generalis when there is in place a lex specialis to deal with the very situation; that is to say, a situation where a statement is to be tendered in lieu of oral evidence. But the bottom line is: Nobody ever asked for it. And those are our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kremer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: In response to the question of the application of 89(F), our position is and we agree with Mr. Emmerson on this point, that 89(F) is a general rule and Rules 92, 92 bis, 92 ter, and 92 quater are legis specialis. However, I -- we disagree with Mr. Emmerson's submissions that Rule 89(F) is of no meaning at all in respect of matters that it -- that are not contemplated within Rule 92, 92 bis, 92 ter, or 92 quater. Because as the Milosevic decision shows, the genesis for 92 ter was the appeals decision in 92 quater. At the time not only was the 92 ter introduced, but 92 quater was also introduced as a result of the Appeals Chamber's formulation that there were other circumstances that would obtain specifically for the introduction of written evidence or evidence in a written form in the interests of justice. Our position is, quite simply, that the Rules define what specific examples have been identified by this Court as covering the interests of justice in terms of the introduction of evidence in a written form, and they provide clear guidance to Trial Chambers as to how and when this evidence can be introduced. That does not mean that evidence that was not contemplated and that has not been contemplated and drafted and incorporated into the Rules does not fall within 89(F). Otherwise, the term "where the interests of justice allow" would have no meaning. Our position is that witness intimidation was -- is not covered in Rules 92, 92 bis, 92 ter, and 92 quater. Witness intimidation is a problem that arose in this case that confronted the Trial Chamber and that it could have and should have dealt with in terms of what to do with the evidence that was being excluded. The Trial Chamber saw fit to close the trial and not hear the evidence so that this large piece of evidence is missing. Mr. Emmerson would suggest and his remarks reflect a characterisation of the witness evidence and the witnesses as reluctant witnesses. I think it is clear from the record that these witnesses were much more than reluctant. They were unwilling to testify for a reason, and that reason was fear. Even though Kabashi says, "I was not fearful," he does say in his transcript that there were threats that influenced his refusal to testify. The Trial Chamber by its own admission concedes that fear and for the safety of a witness and fear for the safety of their families was a central and prominent feature of the evidence in this case. And our position is that taking a very narrow interpretation of Rule 89(F) and saying that because 89(F) -- 92 bis, 92 ter, 92 quater do not address the situation in this case, where intimidated witnesses are fearful to testify, do not testify, and their evidence is otherwise not available, that that allows the intimidator to win and that is what this Trial Chamber and he's asking the Appeals Chamber to sanction. And our position is that there is a fundamental problem in an international criminal tribunal if witnesses can be intimidated, if evidence can be lost, and the Rules are interpreted in such a narrow way as to not to find a way to receive their evidence subject to the conditions that would justify a finding that the trial was fair to the Defence. We're not saying that the evidence should go in and be accepted fully, but that is a decision that should be taken having regard to all of the evidence at the end of the day, having regard to certain restrictions. How can it -- how can the interests of justice be met in introducing these statements? They can be met when it comes to acts and conduct that the evidence must be corroborated. One can seek guidance from 92 quater in those circumstances. The witnesses giving evidence in written form under 92 quater are not cross-examined, but it may be, although it's only one factor, that the evidence going to acts and conduct may -- is a factor in exclusion or inclusion. And that can be the case in this case too. Mr. Emmerson points out that our application under 89(F) in respect to calling Barney Kelly as a witness was rejected and the Court made comments about the -- it balancing interests of justice. That was not appealed. I can't avoid that; it's a fact. But I remind the Chamber that the Court did not examine its decision in the context of -- or place its decision in the context of witness intimidation. It looked at it in the context of: Would it be fair under those circumstances, hearing it through Barney Kelly, to have the evidence presented as hearsay evidence? Our submission is that 89(F) can create a judicial rule which become a rule of evidence and procedure in respect of witness intimidation that can define the limits of the introduction of this evidence and the use of it by a Trial Chamber. In response to Mr. Emmerson's response, I just want to say a couple of things. One is that Mr. Emmerson suggested that our application of 89(F) and the cautions that should be accompanying it if it becomes a judicial rule should use 92 bis as a guidance. I didn't say that nor did I intend to say that if I did. I said the Court should be using 92 quater as guidance because that is the closest application to a situation where similar to this where witnesses are unwilling to testify because they're intimidated or witnesses are unable to testify because they're either ill, deceased, or not able to be located. During the course of his response, Mr. Emmerson raised a number of specific failings, he says, about what the Prosecution didn't do in its pursuit of this evidence. He argues that it was sufficient for the Chamber to provide the Prosecution with a fair and reasonable opportunity to present its case. And the Prosecution was presented with opportunities to present its case in respect of these two witnesses. The record is clear. There was -- there were extended efforts to bring Shefqet Kabashi before the Trial Chamber. He testified once in The Hague before he was released and escaped -- or returned to his home country. The Trial Chamber took over the matter and remained seized of the matter for several months before turning it back to the parties, and it was at that time that the party -- the Prosecution sought videolink evidence. The Trial Chamber allowed that. But at the end of the day, the measures that might have compelled him to testify - although I admit that he was steadfast in his statement that he would go to jail instead of testifying -- the final process in terms of bringing him before a court and giving him that option was never followed. With the other witness, his illness delayed that process from continuing and it was never followed. But in the circumstances of witness intimidation as opposed to a reluctant witness, our position is the Prosecution or the Trial Chamber was required to do more. If it was simply a case of two reluctant witnesses, we wouldn't have this appeal. It is because the Trial Chamber itself acknowledged that fear was central and a prominent -- and played a prominent part in the trial that we are here, that witness intimidation should not win over finding the truth. And that is why we're hear making the submissions under Rule 89(F) and that is why we say that the trial was unfair because in the Prosecution's submission witness intimidation won in this case and led to the acquittal of at least two of the accused and all three of them on several counts. What should have been the focus of the Trial Chamber was not that they were reluctant to testify. What should have been the focus should have been the root for their unwillingness, the fear caused by threats against them and their families. Mr. Emmerson and his client's submissions would have you think that it's their unwillingness that should be the main consideration; we say otherwise. Ultimately, the respondents defend the Trial Chamber's actions as falling within judicial discretion and the Tribunal's procedural rules. The Prosecution submits that the litmus test is whether or not the trial was fair. In a Trial Chamber that does not ensure that there is a fair trial cannot rely on discretion or the Rules to reverse the result. The respondents' brief on ground one provides a detailed factual recounting of the exercise of the Chamber's discretion. It points to procedural deficiencies by the Prosecution in its efforts to obtain the testimony of the witnesses. The Prosecution, as our brief shows, uses the same record to show the Trial Chamber's displeasure with and obvious futility of the Prosecution in making further efforts to have the evidence of these witnesses received. In our submission, the record demonstrates that expediency - and this is particularly plain at the end from November 20th and the November 26th comments - finishing the trial and procedural inflexibility overshadowed fairness and the protection of witnesses and ultimately undermined the fairness of the trial" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you make that submission notwithstanding the disclosure by Mr. Emmerson of the number of occasions that the Trial Chamber attempted to have the witness testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: The issue -- maybe I can put it -- this simply. The issue of witness intimidation was before the Trial Chamber. The Prosecution had to follow the Rules of Procedure and Evidence to attempt to put the evidence before the Chamber. It was clear that with respect to these two witnesses those procedures would not work or were not working I guess is the better way to put it, because we never know because of where the trial stopped as to whether or not the contempt sanction against the two witnesses, if ever put before them, would have worked. We know that for other witnesses it did, but for these two the process that was required to be followed, given their not being on Dutch soil to appear before the Tribunal, became more complicated and took on delays that were unforeseen and uncontrollable by both the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution. But the ultimate penalty for the procedural difficulties that existed because of the residence of these witnesses because borne by the Prosecution and borne by the victims and witnesses when the result was the acquittal of these accused. In its judgement, the Trial Chamber wrapped intimidation under the heading of "difficulties with obtaining witness testimony." That's the heading before paragraph 22. I would submit that the choice of words and its discussion exposes the main weakness in the Trial Chamber's approach to witness intimidation. It viewed it as a difficulty to be overcome instead of a fundamental fair trial issue to be solved. The Prosecution says that this Chamber has the opportunity to correct the injustice of the fair trial on the Jablanica count. The victims of those counts were denied justice because evidence crucial to the witness -- evidence of crucial witness evidence was never received because of threats. It wasn't received because of an attempt by the Prosecution to subvert the functioning of 92 bis. These were circumstances over which the Prosecution had no control whatsoever. And the record shows that the Trial Chamber had little control. And that is the difference between the decisions in Milosevic and Galic and the application of the Rules that we say marks the difference between when to apply 92 bis and 92 quater and when to apply 89(F). 92 quater was obviously not available, but our submission is that 89(F) would have and should have been considered to remedy a problem that was clear and overwhelming in its consequences during the course of this trial. This Chamber has the opportunity to show the international community that it can effectively deal with witness intimidation and that witness intimidation will not be an obstacle to justice. 89(F) can be a vehicle through which the voices of these witnesses can come alive and be -- and they can tell their story. What weight is to be given to the evidence and how it's to be used in the context of a fair trial in the interests of justice is something that only this Chamber can give guidance on. We would request the Trial Chamber to give serious thought to giving guidance to all Trial Chambers in this Tribunal about how vigorous they can be and how they should act to deal with witness intimidation while at the same time ensuring a fair trial for the Defence. This is an important issue, a fundamental issue, and we would ask the Chamber to be very careful and very -- and to always remember that we're not talking about a normal situation here; we're talking about an abnormal situation which the Chamber itself recognised but did not address properly. Subject to any questions that are still outstanding, those conclude my remarks on ground one. I believe my colleague Ms. Martin Salgado has a few words to say in reply to ground three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kremer. We'll hear your colleague now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARTIN SALGADO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have three points to make in reply regarding the submissions by the Defence for Balaj on the error of fact and two points -- excuse me, three points on the error of law. I'll be very brief. As to the first point, we have not misstated the record nor come up with a new theory. It has always been our submission that transcript page 4043 referred to the soldiers outside the woman's house and that the Chamber was wrong to interpret it otherwise and find that she could not describe the soldiers who came to her house. Furthermore, the record is not ambiguous. The following transcript pages make clear that Toger came inside the house and that's transcript page 3982, which the Defence already referred to, and transcript pages 3984 and 4005. In particular transcript page 4005 makes clear that she saw him there. What sense would it make for her to say that she couldn't recognise him if she didn't see him? The record needs to be read carefully. In addition, she was able to describe the weapons that the soldiers carried that night clearly, and that's at transcript page 3987 to 3988. And finally, the Defence do not deal with the evidence that she heard him referred to as Toger except to say that transcript 4043 shows she heard him referred to as Toger outside the house. And transcript 4043 shows no such thing. The relevant evidence is at transcript 4001, and this was evidence that was accepted by the Chamber when it found that the other soldiers addressed him as Toger and was crucial evidence showing that the woman knew which soldier was Toger. The second point is that the woman did indeed give evidence that she saw Toger after she was raped and that she did indeed see him driving and he was driving a black jeep. And again, we say that that is another characteristic which shows that Toger was Balaj, and you can find our evidence that Toger drove a black jeep at paragraph 85 of the Prosecution appeal brief. In showing that the Chamber made an unreasonable finding, we have at the same time dispelled all doubt as to Balaj's responsibility for Witness 61's rape. Contrary to what the Defence submits, no one else at the scene could have been the perpetrator. She heard the perpetrator referred to as Toger. She contemporaneously told her relatives that Toger raped her, and the Chamber found Toger is Idriz Balaj. Moving to the error of law regarding Witness 1. We maintain that the failure to subsume factual findings under the correct statutory provision is an error of law. What the Chamber did was fail to appreciate the level of mental suffering that followed inevitably from its own findings on the acts that Witness 1 endured. And contrary to what the Defence submits, these acts were not limited to putting him in the well. They began when five armed men, including Toger, forcibly took the witnesses from their home in the middle of the night. They continued with Witness 1 being forcibly separated from the woman and seeing her taken away by Toger. He was then put in a well with water to his waist with no inkling as to what would be his fate or her's and whether the well would become his grave. And the conduct culminated with Witness 1 remaining inside the woman while the woman was interrogated and rape with the aim of punishing or intimidating her. My final point, Your Honours, regarding Balaj's responsibility for committing the cruel treatment against Witness 1. Balaj participated in the conduct that I've just described amounting to cruel treatment against Witness 1, including by taking him out of the house in the middle of the night and later by interrogating him, and I have set out earlier in my submissions the evidence of him being interrogated. And I will just add transcript page 4025 which shows that the two witnesses were asked the same questions and therefore that they were interrogated by the same man. And for this reason, we say you should find him guilty of committing cruel treatment against Witness 1. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
