utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, my confidence that Mr. Emmerson would deal with all of the matters that you had asked in relation to Articles -- to Rules 92 bis and 89 was a well-placed confidence. You asked at the outset that we should not repeat ourselves. I trust that you'll stop me if I appear to be doing so. You asked that we not read through what we have already provided to Your Honours in -- am I getting slightly dark in here? There seems to be some dimming of the lights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I can still read. Thank you. I'm going to go straight, if I may, to the issues of credibility which are crucial to our appeal against conviction, and they begin at our appeal brief in paragraph 22. And may I say that all of the credibility issues that are raised by Mr. Brahimaj relate to Witnesses 3 and 6. We say in respect of each of these witnesses that the numerous inconsistencies in their individual testimony made each of them unreliable. We have set out each of the separate indicia of unreliability and each of these, we believe, provides strong grounds for reversal in and of itself. However, these separate points also have to be viewed cumulatively. Having done so, we say that no reasonable tribunal of fact have concluded that either Witness 3 or Witness 6 was a witness upon whose testimony a finding of guilty beyond reasonable doubt could reliably be made. We say that in respect of certain key points upon which a reasonable Tribunal would expect these witnesses to have agreed with each other and to have corroborated each other; in fact, they contradicted each other irreconcilably. Further, in certain instances where the Trial Chamber was faced with the clear weakness in the testimony of one witness, they sought to bolster that witness's unreliable testimony by adopting the testimony of the other, and this was done to such a degree as to make convictions based on the testimony of those witnesses unsafe. Going straight to Witness 6 and to the first -- and Your Honours may feel in some respects the most important ground, which is the Prosecution's failure to comply with its duty under Rule 68 to disclose documents in a timely fashion to enable the Defence to prepare adequately for trial. At this point I would pray in aid also the appeal brief filed on behalf of Mr. Balaj which goes into rather greater detail on the issue of Rule 68 violations which occurred throughout the conduct of this case, especially at paragraphs 47 to 55 of the Balaj appeal brief -- I'm sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I may be in error. I may be referring to the final brief. I will come back to Your Honours, if I may, on that particular point. I'll summarise it briefly. It's also set out to some further degree in our reply brief in paragraphs 2 to 10. Essentially it's this: Witness 6 began his testimony at the very end of the day on Thursday, the 31st of May. He continued on the -- for the full hearing on Friday, the 1st of June, and he concluded his testimony on Monday, the 4th of June. During my cross-examination of him, he denied that he was ever in the police reserve and he explained that he had too large a family to have time for that. He denied that he knew a lot of police officers. And he affirmatively stated that he was "a mere farmer and I had nothing to do with them, neither the police nor the army." On re-direct examination by the Prosecution, he was asked what he understood the KLA to have said to him when, as he alleged, he told them -- they told him that he had stayed with the Serbs. To that specific question his reply was as follows -- I'm sorry, the specific question put to him by Mr. Di Fazio for the Prosecution was: "Witness, I'm not asking you if anything they said about you is true or not, I'm not asking you that and you've told us already we've heard you loud and clear. Forget if it's true or not. I'm not interested. What I wanted to know is: How did you understand that allegation? What is it that you were supposed to be doing? How did you understand that?" The witness answered that he thought that they were telling him they believed he was a "spy for Serbia." And that they did not consider him to be Albanian and "they were trying -- kind of trying to make fun of me." The point here is this, that unknown to me, unknown to my team at this juncture in my cross-examination and at the time of re-examination by the OTP, near the end of my cross-examination -- in fact, with eight minutes of the day left to go, at 12.52 p.m., the Prosecution served notification of disclosure on the Defence by e-mail which was received on the 4th of June, 2007. The disclosure wasn't specifically called to our attention, but what it did contain was a document which alleged that Witness 6 was not only a police officer but he was directly involved in police activities. The late production of that information clearly violated the Prosecution's duty of disclosure under Rule 68, and because of it we were entirely foreclosed from confronting Witness 6 with this information. More troubling still is the fact that in re-direct Mr. Di Fazio focused only on the question of what the witness understood and said expressly: "I do not want you to tell us whether it's true or not." When the Prosecution at that time was in the possession of information which may have suggested the contrary. So it is our submission that the Prosecution at that point had an affirmative duty to correct the testimony, if need be, but rather than doing so the redirect was constructed to avoid eliciting the information from Witness 6. We say that by failing to disclose this document, this was a document which was capable of leading the Trial Chamber to the conclusion that this witness was, A, taking part in hostilities; and B, lying when he said he was not. We say that the Prosecution's duty was to disclose that document in a timely fashion and given that they did know the content of the document and we did not, they should not have allowed his, we say, false testimony, his denial of his knowledge of any relationship with the police, to remain uncorrected on the record. We say they should not be rewarded for those failures with a conviction in this case. Their response brief at paragraphs 21 and 22 is simply dismissive of the relevance of this entire point. They gloss over their failures by boldly claiming they complied with their obligations on the 31st of May, the very first day that the witness began to testify, by disclosing the document to the Defence, albeit in untranslated form, in languages that none of my team speak. They then disclosed it in translation eight minutes before the witness was due to finish his testimony at a time when, as the Prosecution well know, we were all under some pressure to complete our questioning of witnesses within the time allotted by the Trial Chamber. So there was no question of the witness coming back the next day for further questioning. Indeed, the next day I sought to raise it. I was told that the witness had already returned whence he had come. They disclosed it in translation when it was too late for us, on behalf of the Defence, to make any use of this document. Cross-examining a witness, as Your Honours well know, takes weeks of careful analysis and preparation in a case like this when this is a key witness for the Prosecution. We need to use the totality of the relevant documents disclosed by the Prosecution in preparing our cross-examination, and any document from whatever source which tends to show that a witness like this was directly or indirectly linked to the Serbian police or security forces was arguably central to his credibility. When the Defence is placed under stringent time constraints for cross-examination and when information of relevance to that cross-examination is withheld by the Prosecution until it's too late, then we say that the rights of the accused are violated -- his rights under the Statute of the ICTY, particularly at Article 21(4)(e), the crucial issues relating to this witness's credibility were: Firstly, whether at the time of the events complained of he was, as he claimed, a simple farmer, an innocent civilian, or whether he was indeed an armed agent of the Serbian security forces inside Kosovo and possibly a spy on an intelligence-gathering mission. Secondly, whether at the time he was here in this Trial Chamber, in this very room, giving his testimony, he was or may have been continuing to act even then on the orders of or under an incentive to please Serbian forces outside Kosovo. This is not far-fetched. The Defence had two concrete pieces of evidence that showed his formal links with the Serbian forces, and one piece of evidence indicating his continuing contact with those forces up to the date of trial itself. The formal links, he was carrying a police-issued Yugoslav army pistol together with a police-issued fire-arm authorisation when he was stopped by the KLA. Although there was evidence that Kosovar Albanians living in rural areas at this time often legally possessed hunting rifles, the fact that he had been given a licence by the Serbian authorities to possess a hand-gun was highly unusual and we say suspect. He was driving his extremely expensive cherished Mercedes and carrying this pistol together with its licence, although he claimed to be ostensibly just out for a drive with his family. The Serbian police, when he went to them after leaving Jabllanice, never inquired once about how his gun came to fall into the hands of the KLA, if this witness is to be believed. There was evidence of his unusually friendly contacts with senior Serb police officers and not just with the village policemen on the street in his village. He had with him at the time that he was stopped a photograph in his car of him taken together with a former Serb police commander from his area. That police commander he said was in uniform. He agreed that he used to have frequent contact with this Serb police commander in his area. And then upon his release he had a friendly, casual conversation, again not just with a local policeman, but the head of the Serbian state security in Gjakove, with whom he was on first name terms. He had that conversation at exactly the time when the Serbs were planning to enter Jabllanice, which they did a couple of days later, and to destroy the KLA buildings, which they did, and to brutally kill elderly villagers left behind, which they did. Within a very few days of leaving Jabllanice, this witness is meeting with this head of the Serbian State Security and his credibility, we say, has to be tested against what a reasonable Tribunal would expect him to say in the circumstances. I asked him: "What did you say to him when you found him?" That's to the head of the Serbian State Security. He said: "Nothing. He asked me how was it in Jabllanice. I told him: They took away my papers, and then he told me: Come tomorrow, bring the necessary documents, and you will get a copy of new papers." It's an extraordinary conversation. He did not at any stage claim that he had said he'd been tortured, he'd been mistreated in any way. He did not at any stage say that there had been any further discussion. His only complaint was that his papers had been taken away. Not the kind of conversation that would take place between a Serb commander and a Kosovar Albanian just released from what supposedly is a KLA prison camp. Is it the kind of conversation that you would expect a witness to recount if, rather than being a poor farmer, he was in fact an agent reporting to his spy master and not wishing to disclose too much about that relationship to the Trial Chamber? I turn now to his continuing links at or near the time of trial itself. Bearing in mind that the trial took place over eight years after the events complained of by this witness. Less than 11 months before he came here to testify, he undertook a long journey to Jagodina in the heart of Serbia driving from Kosovo, ostensibly for the purpose of renewing his driving licence, his Serbian driver's licence. His testimony was he already had an UNMIK driving licence. His testimony was that he did not actually obtain a Serbian driving licence when he went to Jagodina. He was told that he could get one if he went back in three months' time and he never went. His testimony was that he continued to drive on his UNMIK driving licence. So what was the real reason, we ask, why he went to Serbia? Having made this long and expensive journey into the heart of Serbia, rather than obtaining a document from them, he gave them a document. Eight years after his alleged mistreatment, he gave a detailed statement about what he claimed had happened to him in Jabllanice. Two officers in Jagodina who were responsible or purported to continue to have responsibility for the Dukagjin zone. He claimed this was the first time he ever gave any statement to anyone in the Serb police about his alleged kidnapping, torture, and cruel treatment. In that statement, he claimed that the first thing he did when he left Jabllanice was to go straight to the head of Serbian security in Gjakove to report what had happened in Jabllanice. Well, this directly contradicted what he was to tell the Trial Chamber a few months after this statement given in Jagodina. It might be asked why should this individual be so important to Serbian interests? After all, just a poor farmer according to him. Well, this Tribunal does not exist in a vacuum. It is not outside time. It is not divorced from the political world around it. In June of last year -- sorry, the year before last, when he was about to testify, the international status of Kosovo was once again about to become a major contentious issue. Serbia was violently opposed to Kosovan independence and at such a time, it might be thought, anything that could be done to highlight the impression that the KLA was a perpetrator of war crimes may well have been seen by Serbian officers to be a matter of significance for Serbia's ability to resist the international demand for Kosovan independence. Based on all of this we say that the Prosecution's conduct in violation of Rule 68 deprived us of cross-examination material and deprived the Trial Chamber of important evidence which may well have changed its view on the credibility of this crucial witness. And the Trial Chamber's failure in the face of that to give any indication of its reasons for finding this witness credible amounts, we say, to a ground for reversing the decision in relation to Witness 6. If that were the sole basis we say it would be sufficient. We have listed - and I will not enumerate here - additional grounds and many of them why that witness is not to be relied upon, should not have been relied upon. And when that witness said, as he claims to have said, to our client's brother, Nazmi Brahimaj, there will be blood-shed because of this car. We have invoked the concept of the Kanun of Dukagjin which sets out the basis for a blood-feud. Why have we done this? Because this is the most remarkable comment, we would submit, coming from a man who, if he is to be believed, is lucky to be escaping with his life from a hell-hole of torture is instead challenging the man who is releasing him and giving him a receipt for his car and is saying to him: There will be blood-shed. We say that was a declaration of personal war against the Brahimaj family, the Brahimaj clan, as he perceived them to be, and that his testimony here is a continuation of that war by other means. Your Honours, if you'll give me a moment I'm going to skip some pages because I think matters are set out fully in relation to this witness in our papers. I'm going to turn now to Witness 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And in particular to what we say is the fatal -- fatally flawed reasoning in paragraph 445 of the judgement of the Trial Chamber. We say in our appeal brief at paragraphs 75 through 82 that there is an irreconcilable contradiction here between the testimony of Witness 6 and Witness 3. Witness 6 testified that he was present when Witness 3 was brought to the makeshift barracks at Jabllanice. That he was not -- Witness 3 was not beaten at any time in Jabllanice. Witness 6 did not say he wasn't sure whether Witness 3 was beaten. He didn't say that he may not have been present when Witness 3 was first brought to the barracks. He says emphatically he was present. He says -- does not say that he might have made a mistake. He says in fact that there was a very good reason why Witness 3 would have been beaten, because he had family relationships in Jabllanice; that's at 5336.4 through 5336.13 of the testimony of Witness 6. Witness 3 does not say that he might have been mistaken in claiming to have been beaten when he arrived at Jabllanice. There is no rational way that the contents of paragraph 445 of the Trial Chamber's judgement can reconcile the contradictions between Witness 3 and Witness 6 without leaving the reader with the unpalatable sense that the Trial Chamber must have reached a preconceived view of the evidence and then struggled unsuccessfully to reconcile the -- then struggled unsuccessfully and, in fact, ignored the clear evidence that contradicts the view that they had reached. In this respect we rely particularly, as the President pointed out at the beginning, on the principle in dubio pro reo. There is a doubt here and it must be resolved in favour of Mr. Brahimaj. As we go on to say in our appeal brief between paragraphs 84 and 88, the fact that Witness 3 was never beaten at any time during his stay in Jabllanice is further emphasized by Witness 6's accounts of the escape. This is found at 5390.9 through 5390.17 of the witness's testimony. It demonstrates that unreliable as Witness 6 is in relation to what he claims happened to him, Witness 3 is just as unreliable in his own claims. This is further borne out by another witness whose credibility was never challenged, the Witness Fadil Fazliu. As we say in our appeal brief at paragraph 95. The Trial Chamber gave no explanation as to why it chose Witness 3's evidence above that of Mr. Fadil Fazliu and no indication that it considered Mr. Fazliu's evidence to be flawed, weak, or unworthy of credit. But faced with that, again we have an irreconcilable contradiction. One of the most disturbing aspects about Witness 3, as we point out in paragraphs 96 through 100 of our appeal brief, is that he did extraordinarily well out of coming here to testify. His testimony was that he actually had no problems with Lahi Brahimaj. He had no problems with his fellow villagers. But he did manage to persuade the Office of the Prosecution that it would be impossible for him to testify without securing relocation to a very favourable location for himself and his entire family. The Prosecution reply brief makes the point that several witnesses sought protective measures in this case; yes, they did. No one or very few did as well as this particular witness out of claiming to need protection. Where a witness gives the Trial Chamber no evidence about threats or well-grounded fears of persecution, nevertheless manages to secure for himself economic advantage as a result of offering to testify. We say that is a special need for caution before accepting his testimony as being reliable. Most worrying is the Trial Chamber's failure even to acknowledge this obvious point for concern at any stage in its judgement. We set out further at paragraphs 101 to 112 of our brief numerous other illogicalities and inconsistencies in Witness 3's testimony which are disturbing as individual points, but it is the totality of those issues which we say makes this a witness upon whose word no tribunal can safely rely. From paragraphs 113 to 119 we indicate another instance of the Trial Chamber substituting its own explanation for the bizarre and inexplicable conduct claimed by the witness which is contrary to the -- sorry, the Trial Chamber's substitution of its own explanation contradicts the witness's own bizarre explanation. The Trial Chamber asserted that he had gone back to Jabllanice after his first alleged ill-treatment in connection with a Kalashnikov which had not been returned. The Prosecution comments in its reply brief, they say that our argument has not shown how the Trial Chamber's conclusion on this point could affect the conviction. If any answer be needed to that comment it is the clear and obvious answer that a conviction cannot be based on a witness whose evidence is implausible and unreliable. None of the elements of the charge of torture were made out by Witness 3. There was no reliable or sufficient evidence that any alleged mistreatment was due to perceived ties with the Serbs. The basic reason he claimed was because he had failed to return a Kalashnikov. The rifle was subsequently returned and therefore he had to accept that there were no outstanding issues which remained. In the face of that the Trial Chamber's decision on this ground is very hard to understand. In conclusion in relation to the convictions, we say that these two witnesses, Witness 6 and 3 were transparently weak, both of them, the internal inconsistencies in their accounts, the contradictions between them were so serious as to require any Trial Chamber to provide a reasoned opinion as to why and to what extent it found each of them to be reliable. It is the Trial Chamber's failure to explain why it preferred one account over the other when they contradicted each other, which leaves a distinct and disturbing impression that this verdict is not justified by the evidence and that these convictions must therefore be regarded as unsafe. Mr. President, at the outset today you summarised clearly and concisely the issues that we raised concerning a number of matters in relation to sentence. I am not going to rehearse all of those. We had said - and we do say - that the Prosecution failed to demonstrate that Mr. Brahimaj was anything more than a staff officer on the General Staff of the KLA. In other words, not a general, a commanding officer. It is clear that he never formally exercised the position of deputy commander of the Dukagjin zone. In conclusion, he has already served two-thirds of the sentence that was passed upon him and having been granted provisional release by this Chamber he is now studying sociology and English language at Pristina university with a long term view to getting a law degree at that university. His intention is to spend his legal practice combatting all forms of corruption. He is proud of the part that he played in fighting for his country's independence and in resisting the torture, cruelty, and depression that his people had suffered. In his heart he believes that he has always upheld the highest standards of military professionalism and respected the rights of all humans to be without discrimination on grounds of political belief, ethnicity, gender, socio-economic standing, or age. That is all I have to say on his behalf, and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. The Prosecution now. This is Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: Marwan Dalal for the Prosecution. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I will be presenting the Prosecution's response to Brahimaj appeal against his conviction under Counts 28 and 32. Your Honours, this case is about the vicious and sadistic conduct of Mr. Lahi Brahimaj, a senior KLA member, against two individuals from his own community. Brahimaj victimised helpless and vulnerable persons in his captivity for their alleged connection with Serb authorities. During this mistreatment he expressed pure and meaningless pleasure. Brahimaj ruthlessly abused the physical integrity of his victims. Baseball bat was his favourite instrument to inflict pain and suffering. Brahimaj resorted to mental violence as well by staging the shooting of one of his victims after having asked him to commit suicide. He intended and persisted with his violence notwithstanding the dire and defenceless condition of his victims. Brahimaj was convicted for torturing Witness 6 and for the torture and cruel treatment of Witness 3. He was sentenced to a single sentence of six years' imprisonment. The essence of Brahimaj's appeal, as we've just heard, is his challenge to the Chamber's conclusion that his victims, Witnesses 6 and 3, were credible witnesses. In today's submission I will first present the Chamber's main considerations when evaluating the testimonies of Witnesses 6 and 3 and demonstrate that they were in line with the jurisprudence of the Appeals Chamber. Second, I will respond specifically to some of Brahimaj's arguments which contest his conviction under Counts 28 and 32, bearing in mind that the Prosecution has provided sufficient response to Brahimaj's appellate challenges in its written submissions. With respect to the evaluation of the testimonies of Witnesses 6 and 3, the Trial Chamber properly evaluated the credibility of Witness 6 and Witness 3. It followed the Appeals Chamber jurisprudence and took into account the relevant consideration in its evaluation of their credibility such as: The witnesses' demeanour, whether they had an underlying motive to give a certain version of the events, the internal consistency of their evidence and whether they were corroborated. The Trial Chamber granted appropriate weight to minor discrepancies between the witnesses' testimonies and prior statements, given that the crimes took place in 1998, this is in line with the Appeals Chamber jurisprudence in Celebici appeal judgement in paragraphs 484-485 and 496-498, and the Kupreskic appeal judgement paragraph 31. The Trial Chamber properly accepted some parts of the witnesses' testimonies and rejected others following the Appeals Chamber rulings in Kupreskic paragraph 333 and Blagojevic and Jokic appeal judgement in paragraph 82. It also properly accepted evidence on material facts provided only by Witness 6 or Witness 3. It followed in this regard the Appeals Chamber law held in Tadic, paragraph 65; Aleksovski, paragraph 62; Celebici, paragraph 492; Kupreskic, appeal judgement, paragraph 33. In this context the Trial Chamber exercised particular caution, considering all circumstances relevant to the testimony of the witnesses, including any possible underlying motive for their testimony. This is all detailed in paragraphs 13 and 14 of the trial judgement. We are aware, of course, that the Appeals Chamber is very much familiar with this jurisprudence, but given the nature of the appeal of Mr. Brahimaj, it was important to highlight it again. It should be noted, Your Honours, that a Trial Chamber is not required to articulate in its judgement every step of its reasoning in reaching particular findings. This includes credibility findings in relation to witnesses notwithstanding minor inconsistencies that may occur in their testimonies. The jurisprudence of the Appeals Chamber on this issue has been consistent, for example, Kvocka appeal judgement, paragraph 23; Celebici appeal judgement, paragraphs 481, 498; Kordic and Cerkez appeal judgement, paragraph 382, and many others. In addition, Your Honours, the Appeals Chamber grants a margin of deference to a finding of fact reached by a Trial Chamber. The task of hearing, assessing, and weighing the evidence presented at trial is left to the Judges sitting in a Trial Chamber. It is only where the evidence relied on by the Trial Chamber could not reasonably have been accepted by any reasonable person that the Appeals Chamber can substitute its own finding for that of the Trial Chamber. Two Judges both acting reasonably can reach different conclusions on the basis of the same evidence: Tadic appeal judgement, paragraph 64; Furundzija appeal judgement, paragraph 63; Delic appeal judgement, 305, and many others. I now turn to Brahimaj's conviction under Count 28 and answer some of his arguments relating to ground one, subground one, and subground four, and ground two. Brahimaj tortured Witness 6 for his perceived collaboration with the Serb authorities and for his political affiliation. Witness 6 was beaten severely by KLA soldiers on or about 13 of June 1998 at a compound in Jablanica. KLA members took turns in kicking and beating him with a baseball bat. Witness 6 was kept in the Jablanica detention for six weeks. During the first four, Witness 6 was held in a dark room and was mistreated on a regular basis. Brahimaj visited Witness 6 frequently. During these four weeks Brahimaj would come, usually with Nazmi Brahimaj, and beat Witness 6 with his fists and baseball bat. Brahimaj was present also when other KLA members beat Witness 6. In ground one, subground one, Brahimaj alleges that the Prosecution violated its disclosure obligation under Rule 68 by disclosing late the English translation of a document in the Albanian language. According to the Defence, the alleged translated document could have indicated that Witness 6 was involved with the Serb police. Your Honours, the Prosecution has not violated its disclosure obligations. The Prosecution provided the alleged document in its original Albanian language in a timely manner. As Brahimaj's Defence counsel Mr. Harvey has stated at trial with respect to this document: "I concede immediately the original Albanian was provided to us some time ago ..." This is the hearing of 5th of June, 2007, at transcript page 5475. The Prosecution has acted according to its obligation to disclose materials in a language which the accused understands. In addition, Your Honours, Brahimaj had ample time to introduce this purported document and ask to cross-examine Witness 6. He failed to do so. See in this respect paragraph 21 of the Prosecution appeal brief -- of the Prosecution response brief, footnote 60 in particular. In ground one, subground four, of his appeal, Brahimaj has challenged Witness 6's identification of him as the one who mistreated him. Your Honour, Witness 6 properly identified Brahimaj as his torturer. The Trial Chamber asked Witness 6 about this issue specifically. I ask the case manager to put on the relevant transcript pages. And this is the hearing of 4th of June, 2007, transcript pages 5372, 5373; Judge Orie asking: "Let's try to have this clarified. The question was - Mr. Harvey put it to you that Lahi Brahimaj never once touched you physically. And your answer was: 'I know he was there,' but the question was whether he ever touched you physically."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Yes, yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE ASKING AGAIN
utterances.text: "Did he --" And then Witness 6 interrupts: "He did. He maltreated me, he and his brother continuously." In ground two of his appeal Brahimaj has challenged the reasons for torturing Witness 6. Brahimaj alleged in paragraph 69 of his appeal brief that the Trial Chamber erred in attributing to him an intent to mistreat Witness 6 because of his political affiliation as well. Brahimaj contends that the Trial Chamber found that Maxhupi had expressed such an intent to mistreat but did not conclude that Maxhupi was Brahimaj. Contrary to Brahimaj's assertion, the Trial Chamber found that Maxhupi was Brahimaj and that Witness 6 identified him as such. Paragraph 395 of the trial judgement. Further, Witness 6 was clear in his testimony about Brahimaj's accusations to him for associating and collaborating with Serb authorities. On cross-examination, Witness 6 asserted the reasons for his torture, again the same hearing of 4th of June, 2007, transcript pages 5351 to 5352. Defence counsel asking: "Q. You told us yesterday that you were never given any reasons for why you were being beaten. Do you stand by that?" Witness answered: "No. "Q. Did they never ask you any questions? "A. Yes, they did ask questions. They told me you have stayed in the company of Serbs because they themselves stayed with Serbs day and night, and they accused me of staying with Serbs. I was a farmer." See also the same hearing at transcript pages 5397 to 5400. Brahimaj's brutal treatment of Witness 6 and the degrading conditions that he was under left Witness 6 with lasting pains all over his body. He left Jablanica detention with bruises on his back, a fracture on his lower forearm, near the wrist, and an open wound on the back of his arm. Brahimaj's torture of Witness 6 left him unable to conduct physical work or even to lift light weights; paragraph 384 of the judgement. The Trial Chamber closely examined Witness 6's medical condition, including during his testimony in court; hearing of the 4th of June, 2007, transcript page 5471, Judge Hoepfel asking: "My next question relates to your health. You mentioned problems with your kidneys and lungs which you had after your release from this detention. Let me ask you this: First can you briefly describe these problems and how they were caused?" Witness 6 answered: "They were caused when I was in Jablanica, because before that I didn't have any health problems."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: "Can you give a brief description?" "A. I have body pains all over my body, in my arms, in my legs, in my lungs, in the kidney; everywhere, as I said, I feel pain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: "So does this still exist? "A. Yes, yes, I take medication. "Thank you very much," Judge Hoepfel answered. Your Honours, during his cross-examination Witness 6 offered Brahimaj's Defence counsel to demonstrate the wounds inflicted on him by his torturer. Witness 6 said, same hearing, 4th of June 2007, transcript 5331: "I can show you the wound I have that was caused to me by a baseball bat. I am here. I can show you my wound. Defence Counsel Mr. Harvey answered: "We'll come to that." Your Honours, Brahimaj's Defence never returned to this issue. I now turn to Brahimaj's conviction under count 32 and answer some of his challenges relating to ground five, subground one, and grounds seven and eight. Brahimaj and other KLA members tortured Witness 3 and treated him with cruelty. Around early to mid-July 1998 Brahimaj took Witness 3 from a house in Djakovica municipality and brought him to the KLA staff building in Jablanica and placed him in a room. A few minutes later several KLA members entered the room and brutally beat Witness 3 with baseball bats. Witness 3 lost his consciousness as a result of this vicious attack. Witness 3 remained detained in this room for two nights and three days, paragraph 440 of the judgement. At one point Brahimaj brought Witness 3 to his room and interrogated him in the presence of three other KLA members. During this encounter Brahimaj and the other KLA members abused Witness 3 physically and mentally. Brahimaj accused Witness 3 of supporting the Serb police and withholding an automatic weapon. Another KLA member accused Witness 3 of collaborating with the Serbs and threatened to cut his throat. Brahimaj instructed the other two KLA members to practice on Witness 3. They hit him on his hands for five to ten minutes with a telescope. The climax, however, of the mental abuse was when Brahimaj gave his gun to Witness 3 and asked him to commit suicide. That's paragraph 441 of the judgement. Witness 3 could not tolerate his mistreatment anymore. He decided and managed to escape from detention. About ten days later, however, Witness 3 encountered Brahimaj again in Jablanica. Brahimaj, with the help of another woman, again violated the physical and mental integrity of Witness 3. Brahimaj forced Witness 3 at gunpoint to join him to his car, practically abducting him while slapping him as well. Brahimaj stopped the car and placed Witness 3 in the trunk only to take him out of there later and sadistically stage the killing of Witness 3. Brahimaj pulled his gun at Witness 3 and asked him whether he should shoot him. Witness 3 said yes. Brahimaj pulled the trigger but did not hit Witness 3. This is at paragraph 442. In ground five, subground one of his appeal, Brahimaj has argued that the testimonies of Witness 3 and Witness 6 with respect to the torture of Witness 3 are contradictory and irreconcilable. This is because, as we have just heard also, Witness 6 stated in his testimony that Witness 3 was not beaten. Brahimaj's challenge cannot stand. The Chamber considered this purported contradiction in the testimonies of the two witnesses and reasonably concluded that both were credible and -- both were credible witnesses; trial judgement, paragraph 445. Witness 6 did not see the initial beating of Witness 3. In addition, he was not in a position to ascertain whether or not Witness 3 was beaten in the compound afterwards. In ground seven Brahimaj has argued that the Trial Chamber did not reason whether the initial beating of Witness 3 by KLA members at Jablanica compound was part of the two incidents which he was convicted for. In ground eight Brahimaj has argued that if the initial beating of Witness 3 at the Jablanica compound was included in the conviction, the Trial Chamber erred in failing to reason how he incurred criminal liability for committing this beating when he was not in the room when it -- at the time that this beating took place. Your Honours, with respect to ground seven, the Prosecution submits that the two incidents referred to by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 481 of the judgement are indeed the torture in Jablanica, including the initial beating, as well as the cruel treatment afterwards away from the compound. The mistreatment of Witness 3 in Jablanica compound is an inseparable incident. Brahimaj brought Witness 3 to the compound, placed him in the room where he was beaten shortly thereafter by KLA members, and then interrogated and tortured him -- and tortured Witness 3 himself. With respect to ground eight, the Trial Chamber was correct to convict Brahimaj for committing the torture in Jablanica, the two -- the initial beating and the interrogation and torture afterwards, given that the incident was, as I have just said, inseparable by place and context. Your Honours are also respectfully referred to the Limaj trial judgement, paragraph 652. There an accused was convicted for committing mistreatment by omission of a victim in detention camp together with others. His conduct amounted only to maintaining the conditions of the detention camp. In this case, however, Brahimaj not only physically tortured the victim but was also the one who brought him to the detention facility. Shortly after that the initial beating took place. Brahimaj committed the torture in the Jablanica compound without a doubt. In conclusion, Your Honours, there can be no doubt that Brahimaj was ruthless and merciless towards his victims. He brutalised them physically and mentally. For this criminality Brahimaj deserves the sentence imposed on him. He has failed to disturb the Trial Chamber's findings and conclusions. His appeal should be dismissed. With this I finish my submissions unless Your Honours have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dalal. We now take the break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey, your turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will not detain you for long. I'll just address two matters that Mr. Marwan referred to in his reply. The first relates to the absence -- or the issue of the alleged injuries of Witness 6 and Mr. Marwan relied on questioning put by the honourable Judge Hoepfel. The point with all of this type of evidence, of course, is this: If it is uncorroborated, as it was in this case, with no doctor's report, no medical certificate, no reliable contemporaneous evidence -- I do apologise. Mr. Dalal. I said Mr. Marwan. Where it's uncorroborated, no doctor ice report, no medical certificate, no corroborating evidence contemporaneously, no photographs of any injuries. It is an allegation that is very easy to make and impossible to refute that the witness sustained injuries at the time and, moreover, that the witness feels pains and is -- continues to be psychologically impaired as a result. No evidence of any medication whatsoever being taken by this witness. Again, one of those issues where we say Witness 6, without corroboration of that sort, is completely unreliable. But if I may just finish on this point. In relation to the Prosecution's failure to disclose which they gloss over, in my submission, in a way that is glib and inappropriate in response to what is their clear abiding duty. I have been waiting and in my submission this Court has been waiting for a decent explanation for what, I submit, is an affront to justice. I did say, it is true, on Tuesday, the 6th of June, 2007, that we had had the statement. Yes, we had it the previous Thursday in a language we couldn't read. The question that I would suggest needs to be posed to the Prosecution here is when did they first become aware that they had this document. What steps did they take to bring its contents genuinely to the attention of the Defence? Because when they did disclose it on the Thursday before this witness began his testimony, they must have disclosed it knowing that its contents were significant and knowing, moreover, that we could not appreciate what those contents were. Why did a Prosecutor not come to me and say, By the way, Mr. Harvey, you may be interested in this document because it does suggest that this witness was involved with the police? Why was that not said? Why did they not disclose it in translation at that stage? Because they knew that we would have needed to know what it said. It feels like, it looks like, it sounds like gamesmanship. And Your Honours will be aware in all probability of the leading Canadian authority on disclosure and the Prosecution's duty. In the case of Regina versus Stinch Combe, S-t-i-n-c-h C-o-m-b-e, 1991, the three SCR, that's the Supreme Court of Canada, page 326, where the court put it very pithily in holding unanimously: "The fruits of the investigation which are in the possession of counsel for the Crown are not the property of the Crown for use in securing a conviction, but the property of the public to be used to ensure that justice is done." And it's the failure of the Prosecution here, we say, that demonstrates that justice was not done. That is all I have to say unless, Mr. President, you or your colleagues have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We still have the question of whether the Prosecution is considering applying under Rule 115 to have those two statements in the appendix tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] There are four statements in the appendices, two in respect of Shefqet Kabashi and two in respect of the other witness. I've spoken to Mr. Emmerson during the break and the parties agree that it is quite appropriate for Your Honours to consider those statements in deciding the appeal from the point of view of determining whether or not those statements, if admitted, would have had an impact which is essentially the same consideration that you might make if there is an application under 115, could the statements have had an impact. The Defence, as you will recall, in this case did not call a case. They chose not to based on the case for the Prosecution that was presented at the time. And on reflection and thinking back to the considerations that took place in the Office of the Prosecutor when bringing this appeal, it is our view that it would be unfair to the Defence to have this evidence introduced under 115 for the purpose -- and used in the way that 115 is normally used by this Chamber, it would be unfair to have these statements tendered without having them have an opportunity to decide whether to call a case in answer to those statements and perhaps in light of those statements to ask for other evidence to be -- other witnesses to be re-called, to be cross-examined. There are a number of permutations that I cannot address because I wasn't a member of the trial team and I'm not a member of the Defence. So on reflection I say that I was perhaps a little premature to suggest that an oral motion under 115 would be appropriate. I am not bringing such an application. I would -- and with the -- with all of the parties' agreement, we would ask the Chamber to look at the statements in the context of their impact and the remedy that you have to choose would be -- if you agree with the Prosecution's submission, would be a re-trial or nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can the parties agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but the question that I wanted to ask -- but I'll hear from you, is whether evidence can come in by agreement --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I can take the position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- from the parties if it is not otherwise admissible under the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I can take the position very shortly so far as the Defence is concerned. For all of the reasons that I've already outlined, we say that the Trial Chamber entirely properly approached the decision-making that they had to approach. They were never faced with an application which is being mooted by the Prosecution as one which they ought to have considered proprio motu. But they did have before them the witness statements when considering both the issue of the compulsion of the witnesses through a subpoena and in relation to Mr. Kabashi also the various alternative applications to admit his statements under 92 quater and as hearsay evidence. And there's no reason, in our submission - on this I think I speak for all Defence teams - why the Appeals Chamber in reviewing the Trial Chamber's decision should be precluded from having regard to all of the material that was before the Trial Chamber. But the fact is these statements are not part of the trial record - that will always be the case - when the Trial Chamber has viewed material to decide whether to admit it and has then decided not to admit it. They are not part of the trial record and the Prosecution don't seek for them to become part of the trial record, and we respectfully submit that the Prosecution's approach in that respect is correct. It doesn't mean to say that the Appeals Chamber cannot have regard to the statements that were before the Trial Chamber for the purpose solely of deciding whether the Trial Chamber properly exercised its functions in deciding the applications before it. But what both parties are agreed is that it would not be right at this stage for the statements to be admitted as substantive evidence as part of the record to be considered because they could, if ever, only be considered as part of a matrix of evidence relating to the counts to which these witnesses relate and that is something which can only fairly and properly be done in the course of a re-trial. So we respectfully endorse the position that the Prosecution have adopted. I'm not certain whether smuggled within that there may be one remaining area for potential confusion. I noticed Mr. Kremer say that the Defence were agreed that the Appeals Chamber could have regard to the statements for the purposes of determining whether they could have had an effect on the outcome of the trial. I mean, our position is so that it's absolutely clear is that the issue for the Appeals Chamber is the issue that's been put before it by the Prosecution in this appeal. And that is the question, first of all, whether or not the Trial Chamber erred in the exercise of its discretion as to how far to go along the part of compulsion through videolink testimony upon which it embarked at the Prosecution's request. That is the first issue. There is no other issue raised by the Prosecution in its grounds of appeal. What it sought to do - and I'm not certain whether it's entitled to do this without the permission of the Appeals Chamber at this late stage - is introduce a fresh ground of appeal; namely, that the Prosecution ought -- or that the Trial Chamber's ought to have acted proprio motu by creating a Judge-made rule under Rule 89(F). Now, that's a - with the greatest of respect to the Prosecution - that is a submission which is made for the first time orally without notice to the parties. It's not part of their grounds of appeal and it's not one of the issue properly before the Trial Chamber -- the Appeals Chamber, although it is an issue that's been raised in the course of argument. But as Mr. Kremer very fairly puts it, he's not really suggesting, or indeed expecting, that the Appeals Chamber would overturn the Trial Chamber's decision on that basis. He's really effectively using this case as an opportunity to invite the Appeals Chamber to give guidance for cases in the future, recognising that the issue, never having been before the Trial Chamber in this case it would grossly unfair if he were then, so to speak, to seek to impugn the Trial Chamber's decision for not having done something it wasn't ever asked to do. So that's the way that we would respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Hold on, Mr. Guy-Smith, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, please. Obviously there's active thinking going on with regard to this particular issue. If I might, I fully concur in the remarks made by Mr. Emmerson just now, and I -- I fully concur in the remarks made by Mr. Emmerson just now, and I believe that clarifies fully the position of the Defence with regard to how this particular evidence could be viewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Does Mr. Harvey have anything to say on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Only once again to agree with Mr. Emmerson. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber will make no decision now on the last issue that has been discussed. We will address it in the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just in relation to that matter, we are obviously proceeding on the basis that no application has been made under Article -- Rule 115. If any application is subsequently made, then obviously it needs to comply with the conditions of the Rule and we would in those circumstances want to make submissions as to whether in particular it could get, if I may put it this way, off the ground in the light of the fact that Rule 115(B) can only apply to evidence that was not available at the time of the trial and this evidence plainly was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct. That was quite clear by the submissions made by Mr. Kremer. The next procedure on matter relates to the right of Mr. Brahimaj to make a personal statement, if he so wishes. So I'm to ask

utterances.speaker: MR. BRAHIMAJ
utterances.text: Do you wish to make a personal statement? If you wish, you may do so for no more than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT BRAHIMAJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have nothing further to add to whatever -- to what my Defence lawyer said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In that case, the hearing is adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.20 p.m.
